It’s just like making a flipbook, but with Lego. We take a picture, move the Lego a little bit, take another picture. Then when we play them back quickly, it looks like the Lego is moving on its own. Magic! Speaker_2: Can we make the bunny hop? Speaker_1: We can definitely make your bunny hop! It’s going to be a very busy month. Now, eat your sandwiches, pirates and dragons! Then we can draw some treasure maps. Sound good? Speaker_2: Yes! Speaker_3: Yes! Arrr! Speaker_1: (Smiling) Excellent! Arrr indeed! . . . . .. . . . . .. . . .. .. . . .. .. .. .. .. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .. . . .. .. . . .. . .. .. . .. . . ..H.HH.H.

Speaker_1: (Pouring wine) Right, everyone’s got a glass, I hope? It's a nice little Pinot Grigio – not too fussy. Speaker_2: Lovely, thanks, Penelope. Always appreciate a good pour. So, you were saying, Richard, about Saudi Arabia… it sounds quite the experience. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) It was, in its own peculiar way. I’ve told you snippets, of course, but the culture shock was monumental initially. The rules, the restrictions… Speaker_4: Aye, the alcohol situation, particularly. Though I’m sure you’ve all heard my stories about attempting to smuggle some brandy into Cyprus… disaster. Speaker_1: Oh, do tell that again, Bernard! It was hilarious. The poor constable! Speaker_4: (Laughing) Right, right. It was back in the seventies. I was attempting to sail – very ambitiously, mind you – from Jeddah to Cyprus. A small craft, let's say... not built for such a journey. Anyway, Customs caught wind of my little scheme, and I ended up being held. Accused of… well, breaching numerous maritime laws, I think. Speaker_3: (Smiling) And the brandy, of course. Speaker_4: The brandy! Hidden in a false bottom of a watertight compartment. Clever, I thought at the time. Turns out, not so clever when you're being interrogated by a very stern officer. Eventually, they let me go, but it wasn't a pleasant experience. Gave up sailing after that, really. Speaker_2: Extraordinary! And what was it like teaching out there, Richard? Dealing with cultural differences in the classroom? Speaker_3: It was a challenge, definitely. And a privilege, in a way. The students were eager to learn, but you had to be incredibly sensitive to their traditions and beliefs. The most frustrating thing was the lack of discussion sometimes. They’d just memorize and repeat. No questioning, no debate. It was like teaching to a very sophisticated recording device. Speaker_1: I can imagine. You had to tread very carefully. Did you find it difficult not having… well, the usual freedoms? Speaker_3: It was a trade-off. You got access to a fascinating culture, a generous salary… but you definitely missed certain things. A glass of wine with friends, for example. It was all rather… dry. Speaker_2: (Chuckling) I remember holidaying in France once. Took a suitcase full of wine. Needed it for the conversation, you see! Speaker_4: (Smiling) Now *that* is a story I’d like to hear. Though, speaking of magazines, I once had a peculiar situation with a dental journal and a particularly strong gin and tonic. Speaker_1: (Groaning playfully) Bernard, not another one! Speaker_4: Well, I was at a conference in Barcelona, networking, you know. Had a rather stiff drink, and was looking through a copy of "The Journal of Prosthodontics". Got terribly distracted by a diagram of a… a mandibular implant. Started sketching on it, rather enthusiastically, while attempting to describe the intricacies to a colleague. Turns out, the colleague was the editor of the journal. He wasn’t terribly impressed. Speaker_3: (Roaring with laughter) Oh, Bernard! You’re incorrigible. Speaker_1: (Wiping her eyes) You are! You really are. It’s just one anecdote after another. Speaker_2: Well, it makes for a very entertaining evening. Reminds me, I should ask Richard how the students reacted when he explained the concepts of dental hygiene… Perhaps that's a discussion for another glass of wine? Speaker_3: (Laughing) Oh, I'm sure that was a *memorable* lesson, indeed.

Speaker_1: Honestly, the bathroom renovation is driving me mad. I thought it would be a straightforward job, but it's been a saga. The tilers were three days late, and the plumber apparently doesn’t believe in level surfaces. Speaker_2: Oh, you've had that then, haven’t you? It’s always like that, isn't it? You think, “A new bathroom, how nice!”, and then it’s weeks of chaos and dust. At least you’re getting it done. Remember when I tried to re-tile the downstairs toilet? Speaker_3: (Muttering) Don't remind me. Speaker_1: What was that, Liam? Speaker_3: Nothing. Just saying, it was a disaster. You had tiles everywhere. Speaker_2: It was! I gave up after about an hour and ended up putting up a floral wallpaper. It was… an aesthetic choice. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Right. Well, at least it's livable. Speaking of horrors, how's school going, Liam? Still avoiding eye contact with your maths teacher? Speaker_3: He's got a weird face. Speaker_1: A weird face? That's a valid reason to struggle with algebra, apparently. Have you thought about work experience? It's coming up already. Speaker_3: I said I don’t want to do any. They said I have to. Speaker_2: Now, now, don't be like that, love. It's a good chance to see what you *don’t* want to do when you leave school. I did a week at a solicitors when I was your age, and I knew instantly I’d rather stack shelves. Speaker_1: Exactly! It’s about exploring opportunities. Maybe something with computers? You're always on that phone. Speaker_3: Ugh, Mum. People are always on their phones. It’s normal. Speaker_2: Well, it's not normal to ignore your auntie when she’s trying to tell you about her cruise! You were practically glued to that screen when I was showing you the photos. Speaker_3: Sorry, Auntie Val. The internet was buffering. Speaker_1: Buffering. Right. That’s a perfectly legitimate excuse. Anyway, I was thinking of booking something for next summer, you two. Somewhere warm. Somewhere with a beach. Where have you two been dreaming of going? Speaker_3: Somewhere with Wi-Fi. Speaker_2: (Chuckling) Cheeky. I've been looking at some places in Cornwall. Haven't been there for years. Beautiful coastline, nice beaches... Speaker_1: Oh, Cornwall sounds lovely. It'd be good to get away, wouldn’t it? And then I could rope someone into babysitting – maybe Emily? She's getting pretty good at refereeing those football matches your cousin plays. Speaker_2: Emily’s a gem, she really is. Knows exactly how to handle a bunch of lads. Better than most referees, I reckon! Speaking of handling things, you know, your cousin Daniel is trying to get a summer job, it’s a shame he didn’t ask me first. Speaker_1: Why’s that? Speaker_2: Well, I’m friends with the manager at the garden centre. They’re looking for someone to help out weekend’s and school holidays. Could be perfect for him. Speaker_1: Oh, that’s brilliant! I'll tell him to give you a shout then. See, opportunities everywhere. Just have to be ready to grab them! Speaker_3: (Sighing dramatically) Can we talk about something else now?

Speaker_1: (Looking out the window) This scenery’s unreal, isn’t it? Like, something out of a film. Speaker_2: (From the front passenger seat) It is lovely, pet. Absolutely lovely. Could get used to this sort of thing. Peaceful. Speaker_3: (From the back, engrossed in his phone) Peaceful until Dad starts ranting about the sat nav again. Speaker_4: (Turning from the driver's seat) I’m not ranting! It’s just…unreliable. It told me to go down a one-track lane. A one-track lane in Istria! Speaker_2: (Chuckling) You were ever so dramatic, John. It’s a holiday. Relax a bit. Speaker_1: Speaking of dramatic, did you see that chef on that cooking show last night? The one with the truffles? Speaker_3: Ugh, those truffle programmes are so staged. All that faffing about with the dogs, and then he’s pretending he found it himself. Speaker_4: He’s a professional, son. It's entertainment. And those truffles… apparently they're insane money. Better than gold, practically. Reminds me of the caviar situation when I was working over in New York. Speaker_1: New York? Did you ever fancy living over there, Mum? Speaker_2: Oh, I did for a bit. Thought about it when John was doing that big project, but then…well, this is home, isn't it? Close to everyone. Speaker_3: (Still on his phone) Speaking of home, did you see Man U lost yesterday? Speaker_4: (Groans) Don’t remind me. Absolutely dreadful. They need a new manager. And maybe a few new players. Honestly, at this rate… Speaker_1: Right, let’s not discuss football. I’m starving. Are we stopping for lunch soon? I’m craving that pasta with wild mushrooms we had in that little place last year. Speaker_2: We are, love. John's been researching some amazing restaurants. Apparently, there’s one near Rovinj that does incredible seafood. Speaker_4: And they have a rather impressive wine list. Though I do wish some people in this car wouldn't constantly blow bubbles. Speaker_1: (Slightly defensively) What? It’s just a bit of chewing gum, Dad. It helps with travelling. Gets the ears popping. Speaker_2: (To Speaker_4, playfully) Don’t fuss, John. It's just a bit of gum. Honestly, you’re like my grandad. Speaker_3: (Looks up from his phone) Grandad used to smoke like a chimney. Remember that? Always had a fag hanging out his mouth. Speaker_4: Don't talk about your grandfather's habits, please. It's bad enough that the younger generation is addicted to... well, this (gestures towards Speaker_1’s gum). Speaker_1: Oh, come on. It’s just a bit of fun. And anyway... did you read that article about stem cell research? Apparently, it’s getting really promising. Speaker_2: Oh, I saw something about that. Incredible, isn't it? The possibilities for healing... Speaker_3: Don’t get me started on science. It’s all just going to turn into robots and artificial intelligence that takes over the world. Speaker_4: (Scoffs) That’s optimistic, son. The real threat is always a dodgy sat nav. Speaker_2: Perhaps we should change the subject again.H.,..

Speaker_1: (Smiling, leaning slightly over her sandwich) So, has anyone else noticed how ridiculously quiet it is in here today? Usually there's a proper buzz. Speaker_2: (Looking up from his laptop) Yeah, it is strangely peaceful. Must be a slow day for the press. Good for our lunch break, though, right? No battling for space. Speaker_3: (Pushing a salad around with his fork) Definitely. I was dreading it would be packed. Did you hear anything back about that proposal I put in for the student engagement project? Speaker_1: (Taking a sip of her tea) No, haven’t heard a peep. Fingers crossed, though. It sounds really worthwhile. The learning analytics side is particularly interesting. Speaker_2: Yeah, the tech integration side would be a real win for them. I’m still trying to wrap my head around all the platform options. What did you think about that webinar on AI language modelling? Speaker_1: (Wrinkling her nose slightly) Found it a bit heavy-going, to be honest. Loads of jargon, very little practical application. Felt a little too focused on the theoretical and not enough on… well, on how we can actually *use* it for our research. Speaker_3: I thought the speaker was brilliant, actually. Pretty inspiring to think about how we can be harnessing these tools. It felt like a proper step into the future. Though I admit, I may have dozed off for about five minutes. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Fair enough. All those algorithms can be pretty soporific! Speaking of the future… did you see that article in the Guardian about the new generative AI writing tool? Speaker_1: The one that can write academic papers? It’s terrifying and fascinating in equal measure. I can’t imagine the implications for plagiarism detection. Speaker_3: Yeah, and what about job security for researchers and editors? Pretty scary if it gets good enough to replace us all. Speaker_2: (Shrugging) I don’t think it’ll replace anyone, just change the game. It’ll require a whole new set of skills. Adapt or become obsolete, I guess. Digital marketing's the same, constantly evolving. It’s exhausting keeping up, to be honest. Speaker_1: I can imagine! My role is a bit more stable, thankfully. Though I do worry about the ethics of using these AI tools – the potential for bias and misinformation is huge. We need to be really careful about how we train them. Speaker_3: Totally. It’s a responsibility, isn't it? I was chatting to Sarah from HR the other day, and she was saying they're thinking about bringing in mandatory ethics training for everyone. Speaker_2: That’s a good idea, actually. Should be compulsory for all AI developers, too. Although, getting them to listen… (He trails off with a sigh). Anyone else fancy a coffee after this? My brain needs a serious caffeine boost. Speaker_1: Yes, please! That sounds brilliant. The University Library cafe? Speaker_3: Sounds good to me. I could use a little pick-me-up too. Speaker_2: Sorted then, let’s go. Speaker_1: Okay. Speaker_3: Lead the way. " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " " "H.H..

Speaker_1: Right then, just a couple of hours to Magda’s, should be alright. Traffic's surprisingly light for a Sunday afternoon, isn't it? Speaker_2: Yeah, it is. I was expecting a complete gridlock closer to the border. Are you sure about this route though? It looks like a bit of a back road on the map. Speaker_1: Perfectly safe, darling. Magda insisted. Said it’s much prettier than the motorway, and she knows the area like the back of her hand. Plus, it avoids all those awful toll booths. Less hassle. Speaker_2: Fair enough. Less hassle is always welcome. Though I do like seeing a bit of the landscape. Did you manage to sort out the insurance for the campervan properly, then? Speaker_1: Yes, dear, all sorted. Had a bit of a palaver with them, trying to convince them I wasn't planning a round-the-world trip. They kept asking about mileage and destinations. Eventually, I told them I was only driving to Tarnow and back. Seemed to satisfy them. Speaker_2: Good, good. Wouldn’t want any unexpected bills landing on our doorsteps. So, has Magda said anything about what she’s got planned for us? Is she cooking? Speaker_1: She’s promised pierogi. Loads and loads of pierogi. Apparently, she's been practicing a new recipe all week. And she said she's got some homemade nalewka – plum brandy. Strong stuff, that. Speaker_2: Oh lovely! I’m looking forward to that. I’m starting to miss Polish cooking, you know? Being away from it for so long. Speaker_1: I know, isn't it? Proper comfort food. She was saying she’s got a few other Polish friends coming over too, so it should be a lively evening. Should we stop for petrol before we get into Tarnow? Speaker_2: Yeah, let’s do. I’m not sure how much we’ve got left. Don’t fancy running out miles from Magda's. Where did you fill up last? Speaker_1: Was that in Krakow, before we crossed the border? Seems like ages ago now. Speaker_2: Probably was. Right, just keep an eye out for a signpost. I'll keep navigating. Are you sure you're comfortable with this campervan? I know you're not used to driving these things. Speaker_1: Honestly, it’s not so bad. A bit bigger than a car, that’s all. And it’s got a lovely view from the driver's seat. Just need to remember not to take corners too quickly! Magda said it’s a bit like driving a boat on land. Speaker_2: A boat on land! That’s a good way of putting it. I hope we don't end up in a ditch. Speaker_1: Don’t worry, I’ll be fine. Besides, Magda will rescue us if we do. She’s very resourceful, that woman. Rest assured, it’ll all be alright. And pierogi await! Let's hope there's some sunshine for tomorrow. It would be nice to sit outside. Speaker_2: Fingers crossed. It's supposed to be getting warmer this week. Alright, let's see… petrol station on the left… coming up now! Drive carefully! You are a lovely driver. :) Speaker_1: You too!. Just take a break when you like. It is a long stint for you too. :) Speaker_2: That is the plan. Perhaps some tunes? :) Speaker_1: Absolutely, do you have something.

Speaker_1: (Gesturing at the muted TV screen) Honestly, the kit’s a disaster. Like, *really* a disaster. What were they thinking? Speaker_2: (Sipping his tea) Yeah, saw it on Twitter earlier. Pretty grim. Though, I reckon you're always gonna complain about a new strip, aren't you? Speaker_1: Aye, but this is a special level of grim. It looks like something a five-year-old designed using felt tips. Are they even trying? It's like they've just thrown a load of colours at a wall. Speaker_2: Seems like it. Did you see that article about Puma pulling out of that sponsorship deal with the German team? Apparently, the designs weren't hitting the mark. Speaker_1: No! Really? That's mad. You'd think with the money they've got, they could employ, I don't know, a *designer*? It's not that hard, is it? Just make it look…respectable. This thing…it just looks cheap. Speaker_2: Well, it's a marketing game, isn't it? Got to be edgy, got to be different...though aiming for edgy and landing on “a toddler’s drawing” is a bit of a miss. Speaker_1: Exactly! And the sponsor’s logo… it’s massive! It's practically taking over the whole shirt. You can barely see the team colours. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Fair point. All those sports companies fighting over that space, trying to get maximum visibility. Speaker_1: It's just everything’s oversized and garish these days, isn't it? Remember when the strips were… well, simpler? Proper classic designs that have stood the test of time. Speaker_2: Deffo. Less is often more, yeah. Speaking of oversized and garish... fancy a McDonald's after this? I'm feeling a Big Mac. Speaker_1: (Wrinkling her nose) You and your McDonald’s. It’s all those processed ingredients swimming in grease. But... (pauses and smiles slightly) Alright, alright. But you're getting the fries. And maybe a McFlurry. Speaker_2: Deal. Gotta fuel the football despair somehow, right? And I want to see your reaction to the new kit plastered all over Instagram. Speaker_1: (Laughing) You’re terrible. But yeah, fine. Let's go. Just need to grab my coat. And maybe some indigestion tablets, just in case. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Smart thinking. Let’s get going. And I'm getting extra salt on those fries. Don’t judge me. Speaker_1: You always do. Always. Speaker_2: It's my weakness! It’s the one thing I love the most. You know that! Speaker_1: Yes, I’m very aware. Let’s go then! Enjoy your Big Mac and potatoey goodness! Speaker_2: I fully intend to! Right then, let’s off! Speaker_1: Don't drop ketchup on your sweater! Speaker_2: Never! (Winks) Maybe. Speaker_1: (Shakes her head and laughs) Oh, you! Speaker_2: Come on, let's go! It's raining! Speaker_1: Oh for… you’re right! Let’s get a move on then. Right, coat, phone… fry allowance secured, let's go! Speaker_2: That’s my girl! Always prepared! Speaker_1: Always.H.HH.HH

Speaker_1: Honestly, it’s just… relentless. Every single day. Speaker_2: What's up, love? Another issue with the housing benefit? Speaker_1: It's not just the housing benefit. It’s *everything*. The gas bill came through today, it’s ludicrous! Like, £280! How am I supposed to afford that on Jobseeker's Allowance? It’s ridiculous. Speaker_2: Yeah, it's tough all round. Are you putting the heating on much? Speaker_1: I try not to. I’m practically living in a cardigan and hat. But the kids are freezing! And they need to study. Little Leo’s got that history test next week. It’s just…unfair. Speaker_2: They grow up quick, don't they? Remember when you were worrying about what breakfast cereal to buy, now you're calculating whether you can afford a hot shower. Speaker_1: Exactly! And the others... you know, moaning about needing a new telly. They’re going to spend their inheritance, aren’t they? While I’m rationing electricity and praying the bailiffs don't knock. Speaker_2: Don’t let it wind you up too much. They'll always find something to complain about. Remember that argument we had about the telly back in '98. Speaker_1: True, but it’s hard not to feel completely resentful. And then there was the other day at the supermarket… some bloke gave me such a look. Speaker_2: What happened? Speaker_1: I was queuing and he just stared at me. Then he said, “You know, you shouldn't be claiming benefits when you’re clearly capable.” It was awful. I had to walk out. Speaker_2: Absolute cheek. Who does he think he is? Probably spending all his money on takeaways and lottery tickets. Don’t listen to him. You’re working your butt off. Speaker_1: I know, but it just piles on the pressure. And then you’ve got trying to entertain the kids with nothing. I was thinking of taking them to Margate one weekend, but the train fares are extortionate. Speaker_2: Margate? That's ages. Remember those day trips Mum used to take us in the summer? That little cafe overlooking the sea… Speaker_1: Exactly! Now it costs a fortune. And parking! It's madness. Speaking of money, I actually placed a bid on eBay last night. For a George Foreman grill. Speaker_2: A George Foreman? What for? Speaker_1: It's supposed to be really economical for cooking. Less electricity than the oven. And the kids like their grilled chicken. It’s a win-win, right? Speaker_2: They are alright, those George Foreman things. My mate Keith has one. He says he cooks everything on it. Even roast dinners apparently. Speaker_1: Seriously? That's terrifying. Speaker_2: Haha! Well, he’s a bit odd, Keith. Anyway, look, don’t let these things get you down. You're a strong woman, you’ll get through it. And about that bloke in the supermarket… confront him next time! Give him a piece of your mind. Speaker_1: I wish I had. I was just too stunned. I just… walked away. And then I sighed and thought about how much the bus fare was going to be to get home. It just never ends, does it? At least I'm recording these conversations now... for future reference, you know? Maybe a memoir. Or a podcast. "Surviving on Jobseeker's Allowance: a Kentish Girl's Guide." Speaker_2: Right. You'll be famous. Just make sure you keep it local, eh? Don't want everyone turning up here looking for handouts.

Speaker_1: (Stirring her coffee) Honestly, the traffic getting in was horrendous. Sat nav took me completely the wrong way. Ended up on a single-track road, dodging tractors. Speaker_2: (Wiping down a table) Oh, bless. That’s Peterborough for you. Everything's got one lane these days. More houses than roads seems to be. Speaker_3: (Sipping her coffee delicately) Used to be able to drive anywhere, you know. Proper roads. Not this nonsense. The council...never did anything right. Speaker_1: I know, right? It added on nearly half an hour to my journey. And then there was that awful news report about that plane crash. Makes you think, doesn't it? Speaker_2: Awful, isn't it? Terrible. Such a shock. I saw it on the news while I was hoovering. Can’t escape it, can you? Speaker_3: Plane crash... Reminds me of when young Michael, your brother, went to Spain. Nearly didn't come back. Terrible storm, flight delayed for hours. Speaker_1: (Sighing) Oh, I remember. Mum was frantic. Did you get much done here today, Sarah? Speaker_2: Just the basics really. Kitchen’s gleaming though! Had a bit of a clear-out in the pantry. Found some ancient tins of beans. Don’t think they’re fit for consumption anymore. Speaker_1: Oh, good find. I’ll bin them for you. I need to pop to that convenience store down the road later, pick up some milk and biscuits. They've got really good deals on the chocolate digestives, you know. Speaker_3: (Wrinkling her nose) Convenience stores these days. Everything’s so processed. Remember when we used to get our groceries from Farmer Giles’ shop? Proper butter, proper cheese… Speaker_2: (Chuckling) Oh, Gran, you and your Farmer Giles! He probably sold more dodgy sausages than good ones, if I remember correctly. Speaker_3: (Waving a dismissive hand) Nonsense. He was a good man. He knew his produce. Unlike these supermarkets, everything looks the same and tastes the same. Speaker_1: True. Supermarkets are just… convenient. Sometimes you need that convenience. I’ve been feeling run ragged at work this week. Dealing with Johnson and his ridiculous targets… I swear, he’s trying to wear me down. Speaker_2: (Patting Speaker_1’s arm) You're a tough cookie, you are. You'll outlast him. Did you see my hands today? Dreadful. Got a new wart on my thumb. Absolutely blooming awful. Speaker_3: Wart? (Leaning forward with concern) Oh dear. Do you know what causes them? It’s dreadful, isn’t it? Speaker_2: Nobody knows! They just appear! It’s awful. Might have to try some of that freeze spray, I suppose. Never quite works, though. Speaker_1: My doctor said to soak it in warm water and file it down gently. Apparently, you have to keep at it. Speaker_3: Well, you should try bathing it in warm cider vinegar. My neighbour used to do that for her bunions. Works a treat! Speaker_2: Cider vinegar, eh? I might give that a go… Never hurts to try something new. Speaking of treats, did you manage to make that apple crumble you promised, love? Speaker_1: (Smiling) Almost! I got distracted by the traffic and the news, but I’m definitely making it tomorrow. We can all have a piece. And I’ll put on a proper pot of tea, not just instant. Speaker_3: That'll be lovely. A good crumble… that's the thing that makes a house a home, you know. Speaker_2: You're right, Gran. You're absolutely right. And maybe a bit of custard on top?

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m so stressed about the biology test on Friday. Mrs. Davies is being brutal this year. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! I spent all of lunchtime today just trying to memorise the different types of cells. It's not sticking. Speaker_1: I know! And she’s obsessed with genotypes and phenotypes. Like, who even *uses* that in real life? Speaker_2: Exactly! It’s so abstract. Did you see Chloe crying in the toilets today? She's panicking about it too. Speaker_1: Yeah, I saw her. Poor thing. Honestly, the whole year group is stressing. I was chatting to Liam in art and he said he's barely touched his English homework because he's so focused on bio. Speaker_2: Art's been a lifesaver, actually. Mrs. Peterson is brilliant. She just lets you experiment and it’s a proper chill-out. I'm really enjoying the portrait project. Speaker_1: (Cracking a peanut between her teeth) Honestly, the amount of peanuts they give you here is ridiculous. I’ve already eaten a small mountain. Speaker_1: (Taking a bite of fish) Mmm, this is lovely, isn’t it? Proper chippy chips. You can’t beat it. Speaker_2: It is! Much better than the soggy ones we get back home. Speaker_1: Dad, did you ever learn Morse code? Speaker_2: Aye, a bit at school. Dot dash, dot dot – that’s S, isn't it? Haven't used it in years though. Why d’you ask? Speaker_1: Just wondered. Speaker_2: Aye, it is. Just be careful with it, eh? Remember that glass water bottle you wanted? Might be cheaper to buy it on eBay than on Amazon. Speaker_1: Good point. And I need new shoes. These ones are falling apart. Speaker_2: Right, well, let's not go spending it all in one place. And speaking of places, are we almost there? I’m starving! Speaker_1: Nearly. Turn left at the next lights. See that stationery shop? I’m going to pop in after dinner. I need some really good pens. Speaker_2: Pens, eh? What for? Writing endless essays? Speaker_1: Obviously! Though I might use them for drawing too, if I get the time. Speaker_2: Alright alright. Just don’t revert to Morse code in your essays, right? Your lecturers won't know what to make of it. Speaker_1: (Laughing) No promises! You still got that Vodafone signal? I need to text Liam and tell him we’re nearly there. He said he’d save us a table. Speaker_2: Aye, got it. Right, left at the lights, you said? And then food, glorious food!H.H..

Speaker_1: Man, this sofa is proper comfy. Feels good to be back in a real living room, you know? Uni accommodation was… a choice. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! Or we could try that new ramen place in Shoreditch. Heard it’s proper authentic. Speaker_2: Ramen sounds amazing. Let's do that. So, future plans then? What are you thinking after uni? Another degree? Massive career move? Speaker_1: Honestly? I haven't got a clue. I'm feeling a bit lost at the moment. Everyone else seems to have their lives figured out. You? Speaker_2: Don’t let them fool you. Half of them are winging it just like the rest of us. I was thinking about maybe working abroad for a bit. Get some experience, see the world. Just need to save up some cash first. Apartment hunting in London is still a joke, right? Speaker_1: Don't even get me started. I'm sharing a room with three other people just to afford it. And maybe start planning our escape from this city… even if it's just for a few months. Speaker_1: Sounds like a plan. Let me look at the menu... Speaker_2: Right, delivery apps at the ready! Speaker_1: (Holding up a photo album) Right, look at this! Remember this holiday to Cornwall? Dad’s got the most ridiculous tan. Speaker_2: (Chuckling) Oh, bless him. Have you thought any more about those suggestions for trips this year? We were talking about going to Buckfast Abbey last week; it was lovely, wasn’t it? Speaker_2: It was, very peaceful. But we need to factor in those car troubles, don’t we? Mum's got that clunking noise again. Speaker_2: Yes, she does. Think it needs a proper look at. We need to get it sorted before we go anywhere. Speaker_1: So, tell me everything! Belgium sounded amazing in your texts. Did you have a good time? Speaker_2: Oh, love, it was lovely. Really lovely. Just what we needed. Needed to get out. Speaker_3: Absolutely. A bit of sunshine, y'know? And good food. Honestly, the food! Speaker_1: You kept sending pictures of waffles… Were they as good as they looked? Speaker_2: Better! We ended up leaving it miles away sometimes. Speaker_1: Did you get a new phone while you were out then? I saw a picture of you with a shiny new thing. Speaker_2: Yes, sorted that out! My old one finally gave up the ghost. This one’s got a better camera, and hopefully a more reliable sat nav – though I'm not holding my breath! Speaker_3: It's got a really big screen too. We should look into it. Speaker_3: Definitely! Just need to invest in a better sat nav first… and maybe a crash helmet for me. Just in case. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Alright, alright. Speaker_3: ...wait, did I tell you about the guy trying to sell us a live rabbit?H.,H..

Speaker_1: Right, so I was thinking butternut squash risotto for tonight. Do you fancy that? Or too much effort after the day we’ve both had? Maybe try looking at some of his lesser-known poems. Speaker_1: True. I’ll try that. And maybe I’ll have a breakthrough after a nice relaxing massage, courtesy of you. Speaker_2: Just doing my boyfriend duties. Anything else I can do to help? Fancy a cup of tea? Speaker_1: Ooh, yes please! And maybe a biscuit? A proper Yorkshire biscuit, none of that flimsy stuff. Speaker_2: Sorted. Coming right up. So, Wordsworth or massage first? Speaker_1: Massage first, definitely. Wordsworth can wait. He’s got all the time in the world, hasn’t he? Speaker_2: That’s the spirit. Now, what kind of tea are we thinking? Speaker_1: Earl Grey please. With a digestive! Thanks love. You're the best. Speaker_2: Only for you, pet. Now let's get that essay sorted...after the massage, of course. Speaker_1: Of course! Speaker_2: Alright. Let me check booking slots then. Speaker_1: Perfect. Thanks. Speaker_2: No worries. Do you want me to get the tea on while you have a look at it again? Speaker_1: Yeah that’d be brilliant. Thanks! You're a lifesaver really. Speaker_2: Never a problem. Just trying to get you through it. Wanting you to do well. . Speaker_2: Right, teaspoon or no teaspoon for the Earl Grey? Speaker_1: Teaspoon please! Wouldn’t be right without it. Speaker_2: Definitely wouldn’t be. Okay massage is booked for 7ish. You're going to feel human again soon. Speaker_1: Can't wait. Thanks so much! You're a star! Speaker_2: Anything for my favourite lass! Right, tea’s brewing! Now, let's have a look at those daffodils!H.H..

Speaker_1: This lentil soup is actually quite good, wouldn't you say, Sarah? A bit more pepper next time, maybe. Speaker_2: It is lovely, Dad. Really hearty. Thanks for making it. Much better than anything I could've thrown together on a weekday. Speaker_3: It's delicious, Robert. You've really nailed it. I always struggle with lentils – they either end up mushy or rock hard. Speaker_1: It's all about the simmering time, Carol. And a good stock. Though, I do wish I’d remembered to add a bay leaf. I’m really losing my touch, I think. Speaker_2: Don’t say that! It’s perfect. Did you see the news this morning, though? About Calais? It’s just heartbreaking. Speaker_3: Absolutely dreadful. The situation is just getting worse and worse. Those poor people… It’s just devastating to see. Speaker_1: It is. And what are we doing about it? Pointless hand-wringing on the news doesn’t solve anything. Of course, you know the usual political arguments. Always blaming someone else. Speaker_2: It’s so complicated, isn't it? So many factors at play. I’m trying to do a little something – donating to some charities helping with food and shelter. It feels like a drop in the ocean, though. Speaker_3: Every little bit helps. And raising awareness, talking about it, that's important too. Do you think the children are understanding what’s going on, Sarah? Speaker_2: They are, but I’m trying to be mindful of how much I talk about it. It's rather upsetting to them, Leo feels upset but I don't have to do. Speaker_1: Children are remarkably resilient, though, aren't they? They absorb more than you realize. Still, it’s a tough world to grow up in these days. Speaker_3: It is. Moving on to less depressing topics… Has anyone given any thought to Christmas yet? It’s only… what… November? Speaker_2: Mum, really? It’s barely Halloween! Though, I suppose we should start thinking about travel plans. I was thinking maybe we could go to Cornwall again this year? Speaker_1: Cornwall’s lovely. Though it’s getting terribly crowded, isn’t it? Speaker_3: It is. But it's still beautiful. And we haven’t seen Aunt Margaret in ages – she’d love it. Speaker_1: True. Though getting there… all that driving. I may be too old for that kind of journey now. I was thinking about possibly doing a cruise next year. Something around the Mediterranean. Just gentle relaxing. Speaker_2: A cruise? Dad, that’s wonderful! It would be so nice to see you properly chilled out. We should all go! Speaker_3: Oh, that’s a brilliant idea, Robert! We could book a big table. Speaker_1: Hmm, let’s not get carried away. Still, it’s a thought... Has your class settled down nicely, Sarah? Are you having any trouble with the Year 7s this year? Speaker_2: They’re a bit of a handful, to be honest. All full of boundless energy. But they’re good kids, really. And I’m discovering that one of my students is… well, he's really quite gifted at art. I’m hoping to encourage him a bit. It is a lovely thing to see Speaker_3: That’s lovely to hear! Always good to find those special talents. Speaker_1: Right then, more soup anyone?

Speaker_1: (Sipping his coffee, looking slightly exasperated) Honestly, Bryn, this bathroom renovation… it’s been a saga. A complete and utter saga. Speaker_2: (Chuckles, stirring sugar into his own mug) Tell me about it! I’ve been looking at kitchens myself. Though thankfully, I’m dealing with a brother-in-law who, bless him, thinks he’s Bob the Builder. Speaker_1: That’s… something at least. Mine, on the other hand, claims to be a ‘handyman.’ Turns out, that translates to ‘occasionally hits something with a hammer.’ The tiling is… questionable, to put it mildly. Speaker_2: Oh, the tradespeople! You get a mixed bag, don't you? Remember old Dai Jones who used to do gardening for my sister? Solid as a rock, that man. Knew his onions. These days, they all seem to vanish halfway through the job. Speaker_1: Precisely! This fellow, Omar, he’s disappeared. Vanished. Last I heard from him was a message saying he’d ‘got a better offer.’ Leaving me with half-tiled walls and a leaking pipe. Speaker_2: (Winces) That’s rotten luck. Did you get a contract? Speaker_1: A handshake agreement, naturally. Typical. Should have known better, really. Should have documented everything. My late wife, Eleanor, would have had the contract drafted and notarized. She ran a tight ship, that woman. Speaker_2: Aye, Eleanor was a force of nature, wasn’t she? Remember her lecturing Dr. Evans on the proper way to prune roses at the garden club? He didn't know what hit him. Speaker_1: (A small smile plays on his lips) He was speechless. Utterly speechless. She always did have a way with words, my Eleanor. It’s not just the tiling, you know. It’s the grout. The grout is a disaster. It’s uneven, it’s patchy… Speaker_2: You’re catastrophizing a little, aren’t you? A bit of extra grout won’t bring the house down. Speaker_1: It’s the principle, Bryn! The utter lack of professionalism! I’m seriously contemplating just hiring someone else to redo the whole thing. Someone reputable. Speaker_2: Now, that’s sensible. My niece, Seren, she’s got a lovely bathroom. Small, but lovely. All done by a bloke called Gareth – he’s highly recommended. I’ll give you his number if you like. Actually, he did my daughter's kitchen last year. Top notch. Speaker_1: That would be wonderful, Bryn. Absolutely wonderful. So, you’re thinking kitchen renovation then, are you? How’s that progressing? Speaker_2: Slowly. Very slowly. My brother-in-law’s convinced he can handle the cabinet installation himself. I’m trying to steer him towards a professional, but… stubborn Welshman, you know. Speaker_1: (Laughs dryly) I do indeed. Best of luck to you. Don't let him put up any crooked shelves, eh? Speaker_2: I’ll try my best. Speaking of which, did you hear about Maureen Hughes? Retiring next month to the coast. Speaker_1: No! Really? After all these years? Good for her. Whereabouts are they going? Speaker_2: Tenby, I believe. Says she wants to wake up to the sound of the sea every morning. Can’t blame her, can you? After all the noise we endure here! Speaker_1: Absolutely not. Well, I’d better get back to my mounting pile of essays. Perhaps I’ll be able to escape the memory of Omar’s handiwork. Speaker_2: (Standing up) Good luck with that! And let me know if you want Gareth’s number. Don't suffer in silence!

Speaker_1: (Sighs contentedly) Ah, that was a grand curry. Bit too much chili for me though, even for a man from Belfast! Speaker_3: It *was* lovely, Liam. Though I think you enjoyed the heat a little *too* much, you were practically sweating! Speaker_2: (Sarcastically) You looked like a dragon, Dad. All red and breathing fire. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Well, a wee bit o’ fire never hurt anyone, did it? Reminds you of your Granny Moira, she could put down a curry like nobody’s business. You’d be feeling it for days after! Speaker_3: Don't remind me. Nearly lost a night’s sleep trying to cool down after her Vindaloo. Remember when Finn (Speaker_4) tried to eat a metal spoon last week? Speaker_2: (Laughing) Yeah! He was determined. Thought it was a biscuit or something. Nearly gave Mum a heart attack. Speaker_1: Tiny mites are at it again. He’s going to be eating a car next, mark my words. It reminds me of me and my cousin, we'd eat anything we could get our hands on. Reminds me of the time we tried to eat a bar of soap! Speaker_3: (Shaking her head) Honestly. And you’re supposed to be the responsible adult. Speaker_1: Trying to be, trying to be. Speaking of responsible, are we still on for the park event on Saturday for Finn's birthday? Speaker_3: Yes, definitely. I've booked the bouncy castle and ordered the cake. Trying to keep it simple, you know, with the toddler mayhem. Speaker_2: Can I bring my mates? Speaker_1: Well, let’s see how many they are. Don't want to overwhelm the poor boy. And make sure they behave themselves! No eating metal spoons. Speaker_3: Speaking of behaving... I was reading that awful history book Finn's school gave him. It’s all grim battles and horrible kings. How are kids supposed to learn about history with that stuff? Speaker_2: It’s boring! I'd rather read about superheroes. I wish I had superpowers, like flying or invisibility. Speaker_1: (Teasingly) You could use invisibility to sneak extra biscuits. Speaker_2: (Grumbling) Funny dad. I could use super strength to... to beat up bullies! Speaker_3: (Smiling) Oh, someone's got a hero complex. Don’t go getting any ideas now. Remember, being kind is more powerful than any super strength. Speaker_1: True that. Speaking of powerful, I was thinking about setting up a night deposit box at the bank down the street. Just for easy access you know, for… well, for important things. Speaker_3: (Raising an eyebrow) Important things like…? Speaker_1: (Waving his hand dismissively) Just important things! Financial management, right? You know, very grown-up stuff. Speaker_2: Dad, you’re being weird. Speaker_1: I'm not being weird. I'm being… responsible. Which is more than I can say for some people! (Looks pointedly at Speaker_3). Speaker_3: (Laughing) Alright, alright, you've made your point. And what about tomorrow? Any plans or are we just going to supervise the terror that is Finn exploring the garden? Speaker_1: I was thinking maybe a walk along the coast. Bit of fresh air, see if we can spot some wildlife. And maybe grab some ice cream. Speaker_2: Ice cream! Speaker_1: Yeah, ice cream. But no eating the cone. Last time, it ended up all over the dog. Speaker_3: (Shaking her head, smiling) Honestly, it’s never a dull moment with you lot around.

Speaker_1: So, Halloween's coming up then, eh? Always quite liked a good fright. Used to scare the wits out of the little ones down the road. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) You always were a character, Arthur. Remember that year you dressed as a giant pumpkin? Speaker_1: Oh, yes. Absolutely ludicrous, wasn't it? Rolled down the hill, I did. Nearly ended up in Mrs. Higgins’ prize-winning petunias. Speaker_3: (Midlands accent) Right laugh that must've been. My little 'uns are already planning their costumes. Maisie wants to be a unicorn, bless her. Speaker_4: (Eastern English accent) A sparkly unicorn! I've got the glitter glue already, Dad. It's going to be epic. The school's doing a Halloween disco too, which is brilliant. Speaker_2: Ooh, a disco! That’s lovely, dear. Are they letting you dress up at school? Speaker_4: Yeah, costumes are allowed, but no masks. Apparently, safety reasons. Speaker_1: Sensible, I suppose. Masks can hide a multitude of sins. Speaker_3: Speaking of schools, how’s school going, love? Getting much homework these days? Speaker_4: Loads! Especially in maths. Mr. Davies is being really tough this term. I’m having to go to after-school tutoring. Speaker_2: Oh dear. That's a shame, isn't it? Still, good that you're getting the help you need. What are you enjoying the most? Speaker_4: Art, definitely. We’re doing a project on mixed media – sticking fabric and things onto canvas. It’s really messy but fun. I’ve been drawing horses a lot as well. Speaker_1: Horses, eh? Always been a fondness for horses. Remember old Bess, down at Farmer Giles'? Used to ride her bareback, I did. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Oh, Arthur! You and your horses. Getting into all sorts of scrapes, you always did. Speaker_3: Speaking of getting into scrapes, did you ever manage to get that leaky tap fixed, Margaret? Speaker_2: Not yet, sadly. Nigel's been promising to come round for weeks, but he's a busy man, you know. Always teaching. Speaker_1: Nigel's a good lad, though. Proper teacher. Remember when he used to bring us little quizzes after Sunday lunch? Speaker_3: (Laughing) Don’t remind me! He used to quiz us on everything. From the capitals of countries to the types of birds in the garden. Speaker_4: Can we go to that new riding stables near Wymondham this weekend? Please, Dad? I saw they have lessons for beginners. Speaker_3: (To Margaret) Wymondham, you say? That's not too far. We could make a day of it, couldn't we? Speaker_2: That sounds lovely, dear. A change of scenery would be nice. Rest your legs after all that glitter glue! Speaker_1: Aye, a good day out would do us all good. Just like the old days. Although I doubt I’ll be rolling down any hills these days. Too creaky for that now. Speaker_4: You could still wear the pumpkin costume, Grandad! Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Now there’s an idea. Hah! Just you wait. You'll see! Speaker_3: Ah, the old man's back! That’ll be a sight to behold! Speaker_2: Oh, Arthur! You're incorrigible!H.H..

Speaker_1: Honestly, this traffic is dreadful! I thought getting here early would beat it, but no such luck. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) You never beat it to the Steam Fair, love. It’s a rite of passage. Part of the experience, you know. Speaker_3: Tell me about it. I’ve seen worse, but this is definitely testing my patience. And trying to navigate with these narrow lanes... nightmare. Speaker_1: It's worse than the M25, it really is. At least on the M25 you can zone out a bit. Here, you're constantly swerving to avoid tractors and… is that a vintage motorbike? Speaker_2: It is! Splendid, isn’t it? Look at that chrome, the gleam. Proper classic. Speaker_3: Nice to look at, perhaps, but not so nice when it’s crawling in front of you at twenty miles an hour. I worry about my mum, you know. She'd absolutely hate this. Speaker_1: What’s up with your mum? Speaker_3: Well, she's been on the council housing list for ages. Needs a ground floor flat, something with easy access. Her stairs are killing her. But these council houses… absolute nightmare to get. They’re putting people in places that are completely unsuitable. Speaker_2: It’s a disgrace. Absolute disgrace, the way they treat our older generation. No thought for anyone. Back in my day, the council cared. Now… Speaker_1: It’s all about targets and budgets, isn’t it? Doesn’t matter if it’s the right thing to do. Speaker_3: Exactly! I applied for her to go into one of those supported living things, assisted living. But the waiting list is like a decade long. And the prices! Ridiculous for what you get. Speaker_2: Supported living... sounds a bit fancy to me. My sister tried to get my dear old friend Maggie into one of those. She needed somewhere to be looked after, a bit of help with her medication. But they didn't grant her one, kept saying she wasn't “dependent enough.” Speaker_1: That’s ridiculous! Dependent enough to wander off and get lost but not dependent enough for care. Speaker_3: It's all so complicated. And then there’s the parking, I bet. This fair has got to be a nightmare for disabled parking. Speaker_2: Oh, it always is! Last time, I spent half an hour just circling. Ended up parking a mile away and lugging my little Doris around. She wasn't best pleased, let me tell you. Speaker_1: We'll need to scope that out first thing. I'll do a quick search on the fair’s website. See if they have a proper designated area, and if you need pre-booking. Speaker_3: That would be brilliant, love. Really helpful. I just want her to enjoy herself, seeing those steam engines and all that. It’s a real treat for her. Speaker_2: It is, isn’t it? A proper piece of British history. And you youngsters need to appreciate it while you can. Not like all this new-fangled nonsense. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, Grandpa! Don’t start. We appreciate steam engines. Just prefer to take pictures of them with our phones. Speaker_3: (Smiling) Right, don’t wind him up. Traffic's easing up a bit now, thankfully. Good, let's get there! Hopefully, we can find a decent parking spot, and Mum will love it. Speaker_2: I do hope so.

Speaker_1: So, I was thinking about the allotment… it's properly exciting, isn’t it? Having somewhere to actually *grow* things. I’ve always wanted one. Speaker_2: It is! I’m so glad you got a plot, honestly. It’s brilliant. So, what are you picturing? More veg than flowers, I presume? Speaker_1: Definitely more veg. Though a few sunflowers would be nice, just to brighten the place up. I’ve been looking at some guides online, and it seems like tomatoes and courgettes are pretty easy to start with. Speaker_2: Good choices. Courgettes are prolific, though! You’ll be swimming in them. You might want to limit yourself to just a couple of plants. Speaker_1: Yeah, I suppose so. And what about potatoes? Are those tricky? Speaker_2: Not terribly, but you do need to ‘earth them up’ as they grow. It’s a bit of a faff, but not rocket science. Early potatoes are easier than main crop, apparently. Have you got any idea about soil conditions there? It’s worth checking before you commit to anything. Speaker_1: Not really, to be honest. I was going to pop down and have a look tomorrow, maybe take a little sample to that garden centre near the station. They’ve got that soil testing thing, don't they? Speaker_2: They do. Definitely a good shout. Knowing your soil pH will make a huge difference. You don’t want to be planting acid-loving plants in alkaline soil, or vice versa. Speaker_1: Right. Okay, soil testing. Got it. What about fencing? Do you think we need to put some up to keep out the rabbits? Speaker_2: Oh, absolutely. 100%. There are rabbits everywhere! Unless you fancy sharing your lettuces with them. You could go for something simple - chicken wire would be cheapest, but proper wooden fencing looks much nicer. Speaker_1: I was thinking wooden fence actually. Maybe something reclaimed? It feels a bit more… sustainable. Speaker_2: Good idea! There’s that reclamation yard just off the High Street, isn't there? They often have loads of old fencing panels. We could have a look. Speaker_1: We could! That could be a weekend project. So, fence, soil testing… what about tools? I've only got a rusty trowel and a pair of secateurs. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Well, you’ll need more than that! A good spade is essential, a fork, maybe a hoe. I've got loads of bits and bobs you can borrow to start with. Don't go buying everything brand new straight away. Speaker_1: That's brilliant, thank you! I was dreading having to shell out for a whole new set of tools. Speaker_2: No worries! Honestly, the best thing is just to start with the basics and see what you need as you go. And don’t be afraid to ask for advice. There's a really friendly community of allotment holders around here. Speaker_1: I'm excited to meet them! I feel like I’m going to learn so much. So, wood, soil, tools... anything else I should be thinking about? Speaker_2: We should probably map out the plot and decide where everything's going to go before we rush in. Sunlight is a massive factor, too. You don't want your tomatoes in the shade all day. And leaving space between things so they have room to grow… it's all a bit of an art, really. Speaker_1: True. I'll take some pictures tomorrow. Maybe we could sit down with a sheet of paper and plan it out properly next week?...

Speaker_1: Honestly, I'm proper chuffed you came up, Lizzie. Been ages! Speaker_2: It’s lovely to be here, Maisie! Doncaster looks… well, like Doncaster. Nice to see you though. Speaker_1: Ha! That’s fair. So, what’s been happening with you? Still moaning about the lack of decent coffee in Cambridge? Speaker_2: Don’t even get me started! They have this new place, “The Bean Scene,” but it’s all foam and no flavour. It’s a crime, I tell you. What about you? Studying hard? Speaker_1: Trying to. History’s alright, but Modern Languages is killing me. Trying to learn Spanish is like wrestling a badger. Speaker_2: (Laughing) I can imagine. Remember when you tried to learn French? "Le chat est sur la table," you’d say, but with a Yorkshire accent. Speaker_1: Don't remind me! Anyway, speaking of wrestling badgers, have you heard anything from Liam? Speaker_2: Liam? No, not for ages. He just… disappeared after that gig, didn't he? Did something happen? Speaker_1: Nah, nothing bad. He just said he needed some space. Apparently, his mum’s been giving him a right earful about getting his life together. Speaker_2: Oh, Liam and his mum. Always a recipe for disaster. He does need to sort himself out, though. Still playing gigs? Speaker_1: A few, yeah. He’s playing at The Black Bull next Saturday. Fancy coming up and having a listen? Speaker_2: Saturday? Let me check my diary. I think I'm free! That would be good, actually. It’s been ages since I’ve seen him play properly. Speaker_1: Perfect! We can grab some chips afterwards, proper Doncaster chips. You know, the ones dripping in vinegar? Speaker_2: Oh, you’re tempting me. And what about Chloe and Amelia? Are they still going out with those… what were their names? The rugby lads? Speaker_1: Chloe is, yeah. Seems happy enough. Amelia dumped Tom last month. Apparently, he kept borrowing her jumpers without asking. Speaker_2: Honestly! Men! That’s the worst offense. It's like, borrow my jumpers and you've gone past the point of no return. Speaker_1: Exactly! So, listen, I was thinking… we should all try and plan something soon. Like a proper girls' weekend away. Somewhere sunny. Speaker_2: Ooh, I like the sound of that! Where were you thinking? Speaker_1: I don't know. Maybe Cornwall? Or even Spain if we're feeling ambitious? Speaker_2: Cornwall would be amazing! We could go surfing, eat cream teas… Speaker_1: Exactly! Let’s look into it, yeah? See if we can find some decent deals. Speaker_2: Definitely! I’m up for it. Let's make it happen! It’d be good to get away for a bit. Life in Cambridge is just… predictable, you know? Speaker_1: Proper predictable. So, chips, Liam, and a girls’ weekend in Cornwall... sounds like a plan! Right? Speaker_2: Absolutely! Sounds brilliant. Cheers, Maisie! You've brightened up my day. And these biscuits are amazing! What are they? Speaker_1: My Grandma’s recipe! Parkin. You’ll love it! Go on, have another. You’re a long way from Cambridge! Speaker_2: (Smiling) I think I will!

Speaker_1: (Eyes glued to the screen, controller in hand) Right, I’m going for it. Full throttle. Come on, come on… Speaker_2: (Leaning over his shoulder) Don’t crash, Liam! You know you'll hate redoing that section. Speaker_1: I know, I know, but if I don't risk it, I'll never get past. It's gotta be the quickest route. Speaker_3: (Chuckling from the sofa, scrolling on his phone) You’re obsessed with speedrunning. Honestly, just enjoy the game. Speaker_1: Easy for you to say, Mateo. You’re not trying to beat your personal best. Speaker_4: (Looking up from a book) Anyone else feel like a proper feed after all this gaming? I'm starving. Speaker_2: Always, Finn. You’re always hungry. What are we thinking? Pizza? I was craving a pepperoni. Speaker_3: Pizza’s always a winner. Or we could try that Korean place near campus? Remember how good that Bulgogi was? Speaker_1: (Without looking up) Bulgogi sounds amazing. But I'm not pausing my run for food, okay? Just shout if anything important happens. Speaker_2: Very dedicated. You’re missing out, though. I saw on Insta that they have a new dessert - matcha cheesecake. Proper drool-worthy. Speaker_3: Matcha cheesecake… okay, you’re tempting me. But I’m still voting for pizza. Less effort. Speaker_4: I’m easy either way. Just need something substantial. Speaking of food, did anyone manage to get into the final night of the food festival on campus? Speaker_2: I tried! Absolutely rammed. Couldn’t even get near. Everyone and their mum was there. Speaker_1: (Sighs dramatically) Right, nearly through. Don’t talk to me, please! Speaker_3: Dude, relax. It's just a game. Remember that time you spent three hours trying to find that hidden item in Zelda? Speaker_1: (Whines) That was different! This is crucial. Okay, okay… I’m in! Yes! Speaker_2: Told you you could do it! See? Risking it paid off. Speaker_4: Massive congrats, Liam! Now, about that pizza... Speaker_3: I saw a video of some crafter making miniature clay animals. It was so oddly satisfying to watch. Like, seriously, tiny foxes and hedgehogs. Speaker_2: Oh yeah? Send me the link. I’m always on the lookout for things to distract me from studying. Speaker_1: Okay, right. So, now I've cleared that, maybe I’ll take a break for *some* food. But I’m still aiming for the speedrun record this weekend. Speaker_4: You’re relentless. Anyone seen that new Baz Luhrmann film? The Elvis one? Speaker_3: Yeah, I went last week. It was… a lot. Very Baz Luhrmann, you know? All flash and style. Speaker_2: I've been meaning to see it. Is it worth a watch? I’m a sucker for musicals. Speaker_4: Honestly, I'm torn. The music’s great, Austin Butler nailed Elvis, but… it felt a bit chaotic at times. Speaker_1: (Stretching) Alright, I’m officially hungry. Let's order a pizza, then watch Elvis, then I’m back to conquering the virtual world. Sound good? Speaker_2: Sounds perfect. Cheese and pepperoni, right? Speaker_3: Definitely. And I'll go find that clay animal video. You guys are going to love it. Speaker_4: I'm in. Pizza and Elvis is a solid evening combo.

Speaker_1: So, darling, how was work today? Did you manage to sort out that… what was it? The widget situation? Speaker_2: (Sighs) The widget situation is still a situation, Mum. Honestly, it’s a nightmare. Everything’s got delayed, and I'm chasing my tail trying to keep things on track. Speaker_1: Oh, love, that sounds stressful. You shouldn’t be working yourself to the bone. You need to take breaks. Remember what Dr. Patel said about your blood pressure? Speaker_2: I know, I know. It’s just… it’s really important to get this done. The new client is relying on us. Speaker_1: Well, get it done, but don't let it consume you. Speaking of which, have you heard from Chloe and Liam? They were supposed to call about the film night. Speaker_2: Not yet. I’ll text them. I was thinking maybe we could watch "Everything Everywhere All at Once"? I’ve heard it’s brilliant. Speaker_1: Oh, that sounds intriguing. What’s it about? I struggle to keep up with these new films. Everything's so… fast-paced these days. Used to be you could sit and enjoy a nice, straightforward drama. Speaker_2: It’s a bit hard to explain, actually. It’s sci-fi, comedy, action… all mixed together. About a Chinese-American immigrant who has to save the multiverse. It’s wild. Speaker_1: A multiverse? Heavens to Betsy! Sounds complicated. Is it any good? Speaker_2: Really good! Seriously, Mum, you’d like it. It's got heart, even with all the craziness. And Michelle Yeoh is fantastic. Speaker_1: Michelle Yeoh… yes, I remember her from “Tomorrow Never Dies”. Very elegant woman. Speaker_2: Exactly! Right, texting Chloe now... (Taps on phone) Nope, no reply yet. Maybe they’re still stuck in traffic. Speaker_1: They probably are. London traffic is always a nightmare. Remember that time you and your brother were late for your dance recital because of a lorry breakdown on the A40? Speaker_2: (Laughs) Oh God, yes! I was so stressed. I thought I'd missed my whole solo. You had to practically drag us out of the car. Speaker_1: Well, you weren’t going to miss it! All that hard work and choreography. That’s why I insisted. Sometimes, you need to be pushed along a little bit, darling. Speaker_2: True. Okay, Chloe just replied! They’re running a bit late, but they’ll be here around seven. They said they’re bringing popcorn. Speaker_1: Oh, lovely. Popcorn is essential for a good film night. I’ll make some chocolate brownies. Speaker_2: You’re the best, Mum. Should I order pizza, or…? So they…found a loophole. Speaker_3: A loophole? That’s a polite way of putting it, isn't it? It's blatant dishonesty. They should be made to pay, properly. Speaker_1: (Sitting on the bed, reading a book, with two small children, a girl and a boy, nestled around her) Right, so we've been talking about how things weren't always fair, haven't we? A long, long time ago, some people thought they could own other people. Speaker_3: (Boy, around 4) Own them like a pet? Can we have a pet dinosaur? Speaker_1: (Smiling) No, love. It was much worse than a pet. It meant forcing people to work without paying them, and taking them away from their families. It’s called slavery. Speaker_2: Why would people do that? That's not fair! Speaker_1: Well, people can be really unkind sometimes, even when it's wrong. They wanted to make money and get richer, so they made people work on farms and build things for them. They brought people from Africa, across the sea, and forced them to work. Speaker_3: Did the dinosaurs help? Speaker_1: (Laughing softly) No dinosaurs this time, darling. But many people did fight back. Brave people both who were enslaved and the people who helped them. They said it wasn’t right, and they tried to stop it. Speaker_2: Like in a superhero movie? Speaker_1: A bit like that, yes. But real life is often more complicated. There were wars about it too, you know. People fighting over whether slavery should be allowed or not. Speaker_3: Wars are bad! Speaker_1: They are, darling, very bad. Lots of people get hurt. And sometimes, even though people fight, things don’t change straight away. It took a very long time for slavery to be stopped. Speaker_2: Why did they stop it? Speaker_1: Because lots and lots of people kept fighting for what was right. They kept telling everyone that all people are equal and deserve to be treated with respect and kindness. They held protests and wrote letters, and eventually, the laws changed. Let's go get some biscuits. And then maybe we can read a story about brave people who stood up for what’s right. How does that sound? Speaker_2: Yes! A story! With a princess! And a superhero! Speaker_1: (Smiling) We’ll see what we can find, darling. Let's go. (They get up from the bed, the children excitedly leading the way.) Biscuits! Biscuits! . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ....

Speaker_1: Dad, are we nearly there? I’m parched. Speaker_3: Nearly love, just another turn. Keep your eyes peeled for Mothercare, it's on the left, right after the roundabout. Speaker_1: Ugh, I’m so bored. I’ve been playing Stardew Valley for like, four hours straight. Speaker_2: Stardew Valley, is that the farming one? It looks quite lovely. We'll all manage something. Perhaps a little trip somewhere… somewhere snowy, even! Speaker_3: Snowy sounds good. Anywhere but here, really! Speaker_1: (Laughing) Okay, okay, I'll stop. Tea’s coming!H.HH.HH

Speaker_1: Right, so, diamonds are the best, obviously, in Minecraft. Everyone knows that. Speaker_2: (Giggles) But I like amethyst! It's purple! Speaker_3: Can we build a dragon nest outside? Speaker_1: (Laughing) Maybe we can, sweetheart. But first, let’s finish our vitamins, okay? Then we can draw the dragons! And maybe we’ll even invent a whole history for them. Like, what do they eat? Do they have little dragon babies…? Speaker_2: Yes! Dragon babies! And they eat amethyst! And gold! And diamonds! Here you go.H.H..

Speaker_1: Honestly, I’m proper chuffed you lot managed to get a table this early. It's rammed tonight. Speaker_2: Aye, we were lucky. Liam’s mum knows the bloke who runs this place. I think that's him now, rushing towards us. With a guitar case… of course. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Always the guitar. Always. Speaker_1: Just hope he didn't break a string. Good to see you, Liam! Remember Mrs. Trethewey from school down in Torquay, the one with the prize-winning roses? I wonder what she's up to now. Speaker_2: Oh, Mrs. Trethewey! A proper character. Plus, that little flat overlooking the beach… it’s tempting, isn't it? You should come down for a weekend, see for yourself. Speaker_1: I would love to. I’ve got that conference in London in November, maybe I can swing a weekend after that. How's Mum? Speaker_2: She’s good, mostly. A bit lonely, to be honest. We try to see her as much as we can, but it’s tricky. You know. Speaker_1: Yeah, I know. Remember when we all went to Tanzania together? That was… incredible. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Ah, the safari. Look, I know you’ve had your struggles, openly talking about it sometimes helps. Mental health is important, don’t forget. Speaker_2: I know, I know. Appreciate it, son. You always were the sensible one. Speaking of which, have you seen that new show on HBO? "House of the Dragon"? Bit of a Game of Thrones prequel. Speaker_1: Yeah, I've heard good things. Speaker_1: Right, kettle's on. Fancy a builder's brew or something a bit fancier? I've got some Earl Grey, that's a bit of a treat. Speaker_2: Builder's is perfect, thanks. Always the most reliable. Speaker_1: (Snips gently at hair with scissors) Right, so where were we? The string breaking, wasn't it? It's infuriating, absolutely infuriating. I’ve had so many rackets ruined that way. I like that. And a catchy name. Something memorable. "Fleet Strings"? No, that's silly. Speaker_2: Fleet… as in, a fleet of rackets, all swiftly repaired. It's a bit clever, isn't it? A really polished one. And a solid business plan. We’d have to show them the demand, the potential profit… Speaker_1: And a good story. "Two pensioners turning their frustration with broken racket strings into a thriving enterprise!" Speaker_2: (Grinning) Exactly! And you, demonstrating your – ahem – slightly uneven haircut, could be our unique selling point. It’s memorable! Speaker_1: Oh honestly. (Adjusts the mirror) Well, it’s certainly a conversation starter. So, prototype first. Then a business plan. Speaker_1: Lovely cuppa, that. Just right. Been a bit chilly this afternoon, hasn’t it? Speaker_2: It has, dear. Bit of a nip in the air. Though Norfolk weather’s rarely ever predictable, is it? Just saw the colours, you know. The way they danced. Speaker_2: You’re getting cultured in your old age, Harold! It’s lovely to see. Speaker_1: Don't go changing me now. Speaker_1: Right, so farm day done and dusted! What did you both think? Isla, you were practically glued to the sheep. Speaker_2: They were fluffy! And they said baa! And I fed one a carrot. Speaker_1: (Laughs) I wish! Although, even in a commune, I bet we'd end up arguing about the best way to distribute the vegetables. Speaker_2: (Smiling) Probably. Still, it'd be nice to escape the capitalist nightmare for a little while. Speaking of nightmares, did you hear about the latest reshuffle at *Metro*? Speaker_2: So, what did you think of the nursery? Little Leo seemed pretty happy when I picked him up. Speaker_1: Honestly, I'm a wreck, love. Absolutely a wreck. Leaving him there this morning... Speaker_1: You were! And that's why I put extra relish on the table. So you'd have somewhere else to cover yourself. Speaker_2: You are wicked! So, holiday plans? He is still on pouches mostly isn't he. Speaker_1: Yes, mostly. He ate some mashed sweet potato the other day without throwing it all over the floor. Baby steps, love, baby steps. I'm thinking of trying him with spaghetti next week. Just plain spaghetti. Speaker_2: That's good. Don't overcomplicate it. He’ll probably just make a mess of it, but it’s good practice. Are you watching that new detective show on BBC Player? 'Shadows of Doubt?' Speaker_1: Oh, you know me. Always watching a crime drama. It’s brilliant, honestly. Really gripping. You should have a watch. But you’ll catch up on it. Swamped with your essays, I expect. Speaker_2: Yeah, the uni work is intense. But I’ll definitely check it out. And don't worry about Leo too much, Mum. He’ll be fine. You’re a brilliant mum, you know. Speaker_1: Thanks, love. That’s nice to hear. Now, eat your pasta before it gets cold. And try not to get too much sauce on your face, eh?

Speaker_1: Honestly, the day was just… hectic. I’m still processing it all. Speaker_2: Tell us. What happened? You looked a bit pale when you walked in. Speaker_1: It was the police. They wanted a statement. About the… incident at the gallery. Speaker_3: Oh, wow. The one with the… the sculpture? Speaker_1: Yes. Apparently, someone tripped and damaged it. They’ve added some ridiculous premium service I didn't authorise. Speaker_3: That's so annoying. They do that on purpose, don’t they? Speaker_2: It feels like it! I’m on the phone to them tomorrow, ready for a fight. I’ve compiled all the evidence. Speaker_4: Good luck with that! Let us know how it goes. Speaker_3: Right, my week is looking fairly quiet. Trying to sort out the staffing rota at the store – always a challenge. Speaker_1: Oh, you know how it is. Speaker_4: I’ve got a meeting with investors on Wednesday, which should be interesting. Trying to secure more funding for the new app. Speaker_1: Good luck with that. Is it looking promising? Speaker_4: Potentially, yes. The feedback has been positive, but you never know with these things. Speaker_3: So, what are we all doing this weekend? Any plans? Speaker_1: I was thinking of finally getting around to clearing out the attic. Dreadful task, but it needs doing. Speaker_2: Oh, don’t say that! You’ll find a treasure trove of forgotten gems! Speaker_1: More likely a treasure trove of dust and broken toys, I suspect. Speaker_4: I might go camping with some friends – weather permitting, obviously. Speaker_3: Ooh, camping sounds fun! Maybe I’ll join you. Where are you thinking of going? Speaker_2: We should all try to get together for a proper night out sometime soon. It's been ages. Speaker_1: Yes, that would be lovely. We definitely need to make an effort. Maybe next weekend? We could book a table at that new Italian place. Liam? Speaker_4: Sounds good, Mum. I’m in. Let's sort something out. Speaker_3: Definitely! It would be nice to properly catch up.H.H..

Speaker_1: So, how’s married life treating you? Settling in okay with Sarah? Speaker_2: Yeah, it’s… good. Really good, actually. A bit different, obviously. She’s quite… organised. I'd love you to come over for proper tea and spanakopita next week – Sarah might need some lessons in Greek cuisine. Speaker_2: Sounds lethal! Need to get some chickpeas and… Do you still have that mortar and pestle? Speaker_1: Yeah, gathering dust on the shelf, to be honest. I should dust it off. We could make some proper harissa. Speaker_2: Perfect! Got loads of herbs and spices now, since Sarah got into her own little herb garden. Trying to be all eco-friendly and stuff. Speaker_1: That's great! Speaking of eco-friendly, I found this amazing shop in China Town the other day. They have all these nuts and seeds, dried fruits... ridiculous selection. Got some goji berries, never tried those before. Speaker_2: Goji berries? So posh. Are they good with chickpeas? Speaker_1: (Laughing) I don’t know yet! Trying them in a smoothie. And I got a little jade pendant. A souvenir, I suppose. Speaker_2: Nice! Sarah likes that sort of thing. She’s really been into vintage clothes lately too. Finding all sorts of bargains. Restoring them practically. Speaker_1: That’s brilliant! It's good to find a hobby. How’s the gardening going? Any big successes? Speaker_2: Not really. The slugs got to my courgette plants. The absolute worst. And I got stung by sea lice the other day… Never seen anything like it. Speaker_1: Sea lice?! Where were you, the Caribbean? Speaker_2: No! The local pond. Honestly, Bedford is wilder than you think. Managed to avoid malarials thankfully, though. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) You are a character.H.HH.HH

Speaker_1: Ugh, I’m so ready for the weekend. This week has been brutal. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! That English test was a nightmare. I swear, Mrs. Davies was trying to trick us. So, did you hear about what happened with Liam and Sophie? Speaker_2: No! What? Don’t tell me he… Speaker_1: He apparently tripped over his own feet in front of the whole school during rugby practice. And landed right in a puddle. Speaker_2: (Bursts out laughing) No way! Oh my god, that’s hilarious! Was he okay? Speaker_1: Apparently, yeah. Just completely soaked. He looked mortified, though. Everyone was trying not to laugh. Speaker_2: Serves him right for showing off. So, French lessons… still a disaster zone? Speaker_1: They are. Madame Dubois is relentless. She expects us to be fluent after, like, three months. It’s impossible! Speaker_2: Seriously. I can barely say “Bonjour.” I’m thinking of just pretending to be mute. Speaker_1: (Laughing) That’s tempting. Listen, are you free to grab a coffee after school tomorrow? We could brainstorm Art ideas and commiserate about English. Speaker_2: Definitely! Costa’s? Speaker_1: Perfect. And maybe we can avoid talking about bananas. Speaker_2: Deal. And Tennyson. Definitely no Tennyson. Speaker_1: Great! See you then! Speaker_2: Later! Bye! Speaker_1: Bye! Good luck on Friday, gonna be a great weekend. Speaker_2: You too! Same. Speaker_1: Later bye!H.HH.HH

Speaker_1: (Sipping her tea, looking around the café) Lovely to see ya, Maureen! And Liam, good to see you too – look a bit peaky, lad, are you alright? I nearly lost my voice on Saturday shoutin’ at the telly! Absolutely brilliant. The new manager's done wonders, hasn’t he? Speaker_2: He’s alright. Though I think the whole “Toon Army” branding is a bit much. All those flags... it feels a bit manufactured, doesn’t it? Speaker_3: Manufactured? It’s passion, Liam! Pure and simple. A bit of Geordie pride. Remember the days when we'd all be down the Leazes End, singing our hearts out? Speaker_1: Oh, the Leazes End... *that* was something. Used to get a right singin’ voice after a full day of teachin’. You'd be hoarse for a week! Speaker_2: You lot were mad. Honestly. All chanting and scarves and… Honestly, it probably contributed to the decline of the British coal industry. All that shouting. Speaker_3: (Laughing) You're a card, you are! Honestly, the youth of today... No appreciation for a bit of proper atmosphere. Speaker_1: So Maureen, did you manage to sort out that issue with your computer? Still struggling with the new software? Speaker_3: Honestly, Brenda, I’m at my wit’s end. I keep trying, but it’s like it’s actively fighting against me. I was trying to book a doctor’s appointment online the other day... Ended up ordering a new set of garden gnomes instead. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, Maureen! You and your gnomes! You need a proper lesson, lass. Liam, you're good with computers, aren't you? Could you take a look at it for her? Speaker_2: (Sighing) Fine. But I’m not promising anything. And you owe me. Maybe a pint at the weekend? Speaker_3: A pint, a lesson, and a good joke! That’s a bargain. Speaking of jokes… Why don't scientists trust atoms? Speaker_1: Oh, I know this one. Why? Speaker_3: Because they make up everything! Speaker_2: (Groans) Seriously, Gran? That’s the best you’ve got?

Speaker_1: (Smiling, carving the roast chicken) Right, everyone, help yourselves. Bit of everything for everyone, I hope. Speaker_2: Lovely, lovely. Looks a right treat, Sarah. You always do well with the chicken. Never dry. Speaker_3: (Reaches for a large portion of potatoes) Always does, dear. Always. Takes a gift, you know, keeping it moist. I’ve never managed it myself. Always ends up like cardboard. Speaker_4: (Piling his plate) It smells amazing. Though, Mum, maybe go a bit easier on the potatoes. You know we’re all trying to… you know. Speaker_3: Trying to what? Starve? Don't be daft, Michael. A bit of potato never hurt anyone. Besides, you all have good genes. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) That's what everyone says, Mum. But a bit of moderation never hurts either. I was reading an article the other day about the obesity crisis, and… Speaker_2: Oh, here we go. Another doom and gloom article. You lecturers are all the same, Sarah. Always telling us something we already know. Speaker_4: It’s not just lecturers, Dad. It’s a serious issue. Look at little Leo down the road… hasn’t left his house in six months. Speaker_3: He’s probably just playing video games, dear. They do engross you. Remember when your father used to spend hours tinkering with his Morris Minor. Speaker_2: That was different! That was keeping something running! This is just… sitting around. And a lot of it is processed food. You can't blame people, the clever devils marketing all that rubbish. Speaker_1: Well, Dad’s got a point there. The advertising is relentless. And food allergies are just getting worse, aren’t they? Poor Emily’s got another reaction to something. Speaker_4: Yeah, she's convinced it's the new almond butter we bought. Doctor says it could be anything. Getting harder and harder to figure out what she *can* eat. Speaker_3: Speaking of doctors and hospitals… how’s your knee, Roger? Last I heard you were still hobbling around. Speaker_2: It's alright. Slow recovery, you know. That surgery last year. They said no complications, but it's still stiff. Got to keep the exercises up. Speaker_1: It must be frustrating. The waiting lists are ridiculous these days. My colleague’s mum’s been waiting six months for a hip replacement. Speaker_4: It's the funding, isn't it? Always the funding. Speaker_3: It’s a disgrace. Should be prioritised. So, (gesturing to the table) are we doing a jigsaw after dinner? I bought that new one from the charity shop. It’s a picture of Norwich Cathedral. Speaker_1: Sounds lovely, Mum. Though I’m not sure Michael will be keen. Speaker_4: (Grumbling) Jigsaws? Seriously? I'd rather watch paint dry. Speaker_2: Don't you start, Michael. Your mother enjoys it. And it’s good for the brain. Keeps it ticking over. Speaker_3: It's relaxing! And it's got a story, you know, the cathedral's got a fantastic history… Speaker_1: (Cutting in gently) Alright, Mum, don’t launch into a history lecture. How about we let everyone finish their dinner first, and then we'll see about the jigsaw. Anyone feeling generous enough to do the edges? Or shall we just allocate them? Speaker_2: I told you, Sarah, it's all genes. You can eat what you like, but you inherit the ability to stay trim. Speaker_1: I disagree Dad, everyone, even with good genes should be mindful of what they eat.

Speaker_1: Right, so I was wrestling with Moodle again today. Honestly, it feels like a sentient being actively trying to make my life difficult. Speaker_2: Tell me about it! Speaker_2: (Laughs) Don’t say that! The Dean would have a fit. But I get your point. It feels like we spend half our lives trying to convince technology to work for us. Speaker_2: It really does. You know, sometimes I dream of teaching in a room with just chalk and a blackboard. Speaker_1: Bye! Speaker_2: Bye! Speaker_1: Hmm. Speaker_2: Yeah. Speaker_1: I'll do it.H.H.H..H.H.

Naps second. Unpacking… well, that can wait until Monday. Let's focus on getting through today, and maybe catching a glimpse of the sun. Speaker_1: Agreed. A little bit of sunshine and maybe just fifteen minutes of peace. That’s all I’m asking for. Now, where's the coffee? Speaker_2: Right this way. And I’ll make it extra strong. You deserve it. Speaker_1: You’re the best. Truly. Speaker_2: You too. Speaker_1: Oh, and by the way, I got an email from the university about the departmental meeting next week. Can you…maybe take that one? Speaker_1: So, have you heard from your sister’s family recently? Last I knew they were still having issues with getting the paperwork sorted for Zara’s visa. Speaker_2: Yes, just yesterday. Speaker_2: They’re doing alright, relatively. The KRG is stable-ish, at least compared to some other parts of the region, but inflation is hitting hard. Everything’s more expensive.
