Speaker_1: That lamb was absolutely divine, wasn’t it? Honestly, the best I’ve made in ages. Speaker_2: It was brilliant, love. Really, really good. You’ve perfected the roasting time. Speaker_1: (Sighs, looking out the window at the passing Polish countryside) Bit quiet in here, isn't it? After all that gym talk. Speaker_1: Honestly, Mum, it's just so frustrating! The voice recognition on my phone is useless. It keeps interpreting “right” as “flight.” Like, how? Speaker_1: (Sipping tea) That’s a rather lovely marmalade you’ve got here, Bethan. Tangy. Proper Yorkshire marmalade, isn't it? Speaker_2: (Smiling) It is! My mum sent over a batch. You’ll have to tell me all about your favourite exhibits at the Met while we’re out. I'm determined to improve my art knowledge this year. Speaker_1: I certainly will. After a brisk walk and a good coffee, of course. Let’s finish this marmalade, shall we? It’s simply divine. Speaker_2: Absolutely. It is a good marmalade. Now, about those bagels… do you think you can smuggle some back next time?H.,..

Speaker_1: (Slams a tile down on the Scrabble board) Right, ‘Quixotic’! Double word score, corner. Take that, Liam. Speaker_3: (Scoffs) Beginner’s luck, really. You just got lucky with those letters. Like a linguistic archaeological dig. Makes you think about how language evolves, doesn’t it? It’s kinda like rearranging tiles in Scrabble, really. You’re constantly creating new meanings. Actually, I'm thinking about using it with "Jolt" and getting a triple letter score. It requires a bit of rearranging though. Speaker_1: You're thinking too hard! Just play something. Speaker_2: Oh, speaking of books, have you guys seen that new Julia Donaldson one? The illustrations are gorgeous. My little cousin absolutely loves it. You probably just overthought it. Although, I did struggle with Hamlet’s soliloquies. Speaker_3: It's all about the pacing, Chloe. And finding a way to actually *relate* to a Danish prince moping around a castle. Speaker_4: Speaking of relating, has anyone been following the Chelsea Flower Show? It’s on telly later. Speaker_1: Can’t say I have. Flowers aren’t really my thing. Unless they're strategically placed on a Scrabble board. (He winks) Speaker_2: (Laughing) You’re terrible, Finn! Okay, my turn again. Speaker_1: (Settling into an armchair, a slight rustle of newspaper) Right then, Doris, you’ve been quiet this morning. Everything alright? Let me know if you’d like any changes or further development of the conversation. H.HH.H.

Speaker_1: Oh my god, Beth! It’s so good to see you! You look amazing. Speaker_2: You too, Liv! Seriously, it feels like ages. Last time was, what, Oxford ball season? Speaker_2: Really? I didn’t know that. Speaker_1: Yeah, and the little wooden nutcrackers – those are from German folklore too. It's fascinating, really. You work so incredibly hard. And Tom says he'll look after Teddy while you're away. Speaker_1: Oh, he's a good boy, that Tom. Well, maybe I will. I’m just getting old, aren’t I? Need to do something interesting before I end up… you know. Speaker_2: (Rolling her eyes playfully) Mum! Don’t be dramatic! You’re not even old. And you’re an amazing mum. Always looking out for everyone. Speaker_1: That's my job, isn't it? Now, are you sure you don’t want a cup of tea?

Get this place feeling a little less… empty? Speaker_1: Absolutely. Let’s get some tunes going. And then I’m raiding the cupboards for that pesto. You want a cigarette? Speaker_1: (Smiling brightly) Oh my gosh, Priya! It’s so good to see you! It feels like ages. Speaker_2: (Returns the smile, a little breathless) Honestly, it has! Any concrete plans for beyond your placement? Speaker_2: I’ve got absolutely no clue. Part of me wants to just keep travelling. I'm eyeing up a trip to Southeast Asia next year… maybe save up and do it properly. Speaker_1: Wow, that sounds incredible! You absolutely should. We need to make a pact - if you go, I'm coming with you! Speaker_2: (Smiling) Deal! Now, let’s order some food! I’m starving. What are you thinking? I'm swaying towards the truffle mac and cheese. Speaker_1: Honestly, this pint is doing wonders for my brain after that meeting. Felt like I was arguing with a brick wall. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. That was madness. The crowd was insane. We were crammed in like sardines, and then Alex Turner just strolled out and… everyone went wild. Speaker_1: It was incredible. Best night ever. We need to find a band to see like that again. Something with that raw energy. Speaker_2: We do. I’ve been listening to Dry Cleaning a lot recently. Cheers! Speaker_2: Cheers! To the North East, good bands, and avoiding brick-wall meetings.H.,H..

Speaker_1: Alright, Grandma, you still watching that news? Seems like all doom and gloom these days. Speaker_2: Aye, lad. It's a sorry state of affairs, isn't it? Always has been, really, but seems to be getting worse. This Prime Minister… what a mess. Speaker_1: My teacher, Mr. Davies, was saying in school, about how everything’s gone massively expensive. My mum's stressing about the gas bill something awful. Speaker_2: Oh, I know all about that. Gas bill used to be a pittance, you know. Back in my day, you could heat the whole house for tuppence and a smile. Speaker_1: Tuppence? Seriously? What’s a tuppence, even? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) It’s an old penny, love. Two ha'pennies made a penny, a penny made a shilling, and twelve shillings made a pound. Makes your head spin, doesn't it? Different world back then. People had values. Earned their keep. Speaker_1: Well, it certainly sounds different. Anyway, Mr. Davies said this new tax thing isn’t helping anyone, especially not people whose wages are stuck. Speaker_2: Tax, tax, tax. They’re all at it, aren’t they? Promise you the world, then stick their hand in your pocket the moment they get in. Always the same. Remember that Wilson fella? Promised to squeeze the orange for everyone. Squeezed it right dry, he did. Speaker_1: Wilson? Was he a prime minister? Speaker_2: Aye, in the sixties. Labour, he was. Good intentions, but ended up giving everyone a right headache. Had three-day week, remember that. Didn’t like that one bit. Couldn’t get me new coat finished on time. Speaker_1: Right, well this bloke now? What’s he doing wrong? Speaker_2: Too much borrowing, lad. That’s what. Spending money we don’t have. Like giving a child a full bag of sweets and expecting them not to fall and stain the carpet. It's gonna come back to bite us. Speaker_1: Yeah, Mum said something about that. Says it’s going to affect my future, getting a job and all. Speaker_2: Well, you're a smart lad, Ethan. You'll be alright. Just keep your wits about you, don't trust anyone in a suit, and learn a trade. Something solid. Not all this computer fiddling. Though, I suppose that's your generation's way. Speaker_1: I’m thinking about coding, actually. My friend Liam’s doing it, says it’s good money. Speaker_2: Coding, eh? Never heard of it. Fancy that. All these newfangled things. Still, as long as it keeps a roof over your head and food on the table. Just don't get caught up thinking it's all sunshine and roses. There’s always someone trying to take advantage. Speaker_1: True. So, do you reckon things will ever get better? Politically, I mean? Speaker_2: (Sighs) Hard to say, lad. Hard to say. Best not to get your hopes up too high. Just keep your eyes open and your ears to the ground. And watch out for those politicians. They're a slippery bunch, they are. Fancy a biscuit? I’ve got some ginger ones you like. Speaker_1: Yeah, please, Grandma! Thanks. Speaker_2:Aye, come on.And tell me about school again, eh?H.HH.H.

Speaker_1: (Smiling, gesturing to the table) Right, everyone settled? Dinner’s ready. And Liam, for goodness sake, put your elbows off the table. It’s a habit you need to break, son. Speaker_2: (Grumbling, but complying) But it's comfier, Dad. Speaker_3: (Chuckling) Don't let him get away with it, Sean. Manners matter, even when it's just family. Shepherd’s Pie with a rosemary crust. Speaker_2: Rosemary crust? Sounds good! Speaker_4: Rosemary's lovely. Reminds me of the gardens back in Glasgow, full of herbs and flowers. It was so red. I tried to take a picture but it didn’t come out very well. Speaker_3: Honestly, Liam, you and your phone! Put it away for five minutes and just appreciate it. Speaker_4: Blood moon eh? It's an ill omen, some folks say. Speaker_1: Oh, come on Mum, don't start with the superstitions. It's just a natural phenomenon. Speaker_3: Sean's right. It’s beautiful, isn't it? Perfect for a clear night here in Cork. We should take the kids to Fitzgerald’s Park tomorrow. Speaker_2: Yeah! Can we, Dad? Please? Speaker_1: Absolutely. We’ll pack a picnic. Liam, you can try and get a decent picture this time and I'll make sure you're not wearing that ratty hoodie. Speaker_2: (Groans dramatically) Dad! Speaker_4: That’s a lovely idea, Siobhan. It’ll do the grandchildren good to be out in the fresh air. You’re a good lass, minding them. It's not easy, you know, with little ones. Speaker_3: Thanks, Mum. It's tiring, but worth it. Actually, Mum, I was wondering…would you be free to do a few afternoons next week? I've got a couple of appointments and could really do with a hand with Thomas. Speaker_1: That would be fantastic, Mum. A real lifesaver. Speaker_4: Aye, I’d be happy to. Thomas is a wee rascal, but I enjoy his company. Keeps an old lady on her toes. Speaker_2: Granny, will you teach me how to build a proper Lego spaceship? Speaker_4: Now that’s a skill I can impart! We'll have you designing starships in no time. Speaker_1: (Smiling) See? Family dinners are good for the soul. And your manners, Liam. Don’t forget your manners. And Siobhan…more gravy? Speaker_3: Please, Sean. Don’t tell. Speaker_4: Just pass it this way, dearie, I'll put a bit on my plate too! It smells lovely. A good shepherd’s pie always warms the bones. Especially on a clear night with a blood moon.H.H..

Speaker_1: So, what did you make of the Scottish result? Quite a thing, wasn’t it? Speaker_2: Absolutely remarkable. I still can't quite believe they didn't go for independence. Though, I suppose it was close enough. A bit of a nervous few days for everyone, eh? Speaker_1: Indeed. My daughter, Sarah, was glued to the news. She’s got a couple of friends up there, you know. Speaker_2: No, for someone I know. A young chap just out of university. Property management firm. Honestly, the interviewer was… unusual. Kept asking questions entirely unrelated to the job. Like, “If you were a vegetable, what would you be and why?” Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Good heavens! That's a bit out there, isn't it? Reminds me of some of the more eccentric characters I used to encounter in my teaching days. Speaker_2: Exactly! And then he quizzed him about his favourite colour and whether he believed in aliens. The poor fellow looked completely bewildered. Speaker_1: I'd be! You'd think they’d want to see demonstrable skills, experience… something relevant! What did your friend think? Speaker_2: He was having second thoughts immediately. I told him to walk away if he felt uncomfortable. Plenty of other companies would appreciate his qualifications. I had a colleague once, similar sort. Showed up for an interview in shorts and a Hawaiian shirt. Didn’t last long. Speaker_1: (Laughs) People don’t always think things through, do they? So, how's your daughter doing? Last I heard she was looking at moving down to London. Speaker_2: Yes, she’s still considering it. Has a couple of interviews lined up, one with a marketing agency. Seems hopeful. It’s a big step, of course. Leaving Brighton. Speaker_1: It is. But she’s a bright girl. She’ll do well. It’s just… leaving family, you know? Speaker_2: Absolutely. Though, we'll visit. Frequent visits. And it's nice that she’s pursuing her ambitions. It's good to see ambition in young people. These days many are just... content. Speaker_1: I agree. It’s important to strive for something. So, how's business? Still bustling down at the shop? Speaker_2: It’s keeping me busy, certainly. Though these online marketplaces are a real challenge. Hard to compete with those prices. I’m looking at diversifying, perhaps. Some workshops, teaching a bit of what I know. Keeps the mind sharp, you know? Speaker_1: That's a good idea. Always good to have a few irons in the fire. It's good to keep busy honestly. How are you managing with… everything? Speaker_2: Oh, you know. It's... a process. There are good days and bad days. Glad to have friends like you to chat to, though. Makes all the difference. You are a good friend. Speaker_1: And you too, old friend. Always. Shall we put the kettle on? I think we deserve a cup of tea after all that. And tell me more about this alien-obsessed interviewer…H...

Speaker_4: Right, so, Luton's coming up on the left. Anyone want a break? My back’s starting to protest this long drive. Speaker_2: (Slightly breathless) Yes, please! My legs are getting a bit numb. Changing houses is stressful for everyone. Even feline overlords. Speaker_2: She’ll be fine. As long as there are sunbeams to nap in and places to scratch. Speaking of which, I was thinking of getting one of those automatic feeders. Speaker_1: Oh, those are brilliant. I saw one on TV that dispenses treats too! Speaker_3: Treat-dispensing cat gadgets. My life is becoming increasingly ridiculous. Speaker_4: Ridiculously good, I hope! Speaking of ridiculous, did you see that article about the man who ate 77 sausages in ten minutes? New world record apparently. Speaker_2: Oh, goodness! That's just disgusting. Imagine the indigestion. Speaker_1: Think he’ll be ordering a takeaway later though, won't he? Speaker_3: I bet he’s regretting it now. It’s probably made a massive dent in his pension plan. Speaking of which, I need to look into that. My tuition fees are still hanging over me like a terrible cloud. Speaker_4: Don't worry yourself about that yet, son. Things will sort themselves out. Plenty of time to sweat the small stuff. Speaker_2: You're trying to sound wise, David. Just admit you're avoiding talking about the packing. Speaker_4: Alright, alright, you got me. It's a mammoth task. I've been trying to sort through those old computers. Found a ZX Spectrum from the eighties! Speaker_1: Oh wow! I used to have one of those. Remember Pac-Man? Speaker_3: You guys are speaking a different language. It’s like ancient history. I’m more of a PlayStation man myself. Speaker_2: You’ll appreciate the novelty of it, dear. Nostalgia's a powerful thing. It's why I’m holding onto all those old board games, even though we barely play them. Speaker_1: I still love a good game of Monopoly, though. Just… don’t let Dad buy Park Lane. He gets ruthless. Speaker_4: Hey! I'm strategically minded! The key to Monopoly is owning the railroads and charging exorbitant rents. It’s a lesson in capitalism! Speaker_3: You're terrifying, Dad. It’s a game, not a declaration of war. And speaking of warfare, this traffic is getting ridiculous. Speaker_2: Well, here’s the services. Let's go grab that coffee before Dad starts lecturing us about interest rates again.H.H..

Speaker_1: Right, grandad, are you sure you’re alright with me driving like this? It's a bit bumpy, innit. Speaker_2: Aye, lass, I'm fine. Been on worse roads than this in me day. Back when they were building the motorway up to Manchester, roads were a disgrace. Absolutely disgraceful, they were. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Were you driving then, Grandad? Speaker_2: Oh, aye. Had a Morris Minor. Bright red it was. Nothing like these fancy motors you’ve got. Reliable, though. Wouldn't let you down. Speaker_1: This one's reliable enough, mostly. Just a bit…agricultural around the edges at the moment. Did you see that sheep back there, Liam? Speaker_3: Briefly. Looked like it was giving us the eye. Speaker_2: Aye, they do that. Bold as brass, sheep are. Used to see ‘em wandering along the main road back home, causing chaos. One time, a whole flock blocked the road. Took the farmer an hour to round ‘em all up. Speaker_2: Llamas. Fancy name for a glorified donkey, that. Alpacas, though… always struck me as a bit standoffish. Proper posh farm animals. Speaker_1: They were definitely giving us the side-eye. I think they were judging my car. Speaker_3: They probably were. It could use a wash. Speaker_1: Don’t remind me. I’ll get around to it. Are you comfortable, Grandad? Want me to pull over? Speaker_2: No, lass, I’m alright. Just keep moving. These country lanes are a bit tighter than I’m used to, mind. Never had to navigate roads like this in my Morris Minor. Mostly just city streets and motorways. Speaker_3: It’s a lovely drive, though. The scenery's really nice. Speaker_1: It is. Makes you appreciate getting out of the city a bit. Although I do miss a good coffee shop. Speaker_2: Coffee shops. What nonsense. A good cup of tea and a biscuit does the trick. That's all you need. Speaker_3: (Laughing) You’re a man of simple pleasures, Grandad. Speaker_1: Right you both. Let’s just hope we don’t see any more wandering livestock. I'm not keen on a close encounter with a cow today. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Heard tell of a farmer who kept goats. They used to jump on the roofs of cars. Speaker_1: No way! Speaker_3: Seriously? Speaker_2: Aye, seriously. Naughty goats, they were. Naughty as anything. Speaker_1: Right, I’m sticking to alpacas, thanks. Less… acrobatic. Right, you two. Should I put some music on or...? Speaker_3: Yeah, that'd be good. Something upbeat. Speaker_2: Oh, not too loud, lass. My ears aren't what they used to be. Speaker_1: Sorted. Something mellow then. And Grandad, just a heads up, I’m taking a corner a bit sharp now. Hold on tight! Speaker_2: Steady on, lass! Steady on! Speaker_3: You’re doing great! Just keep it smooth.H.,H..

Speaker_1: (Smiling, gesturing to the table laden with food) Right then, everyone dig in! I made that roasted vegetable tart you all like, and Michael, you promised to bring your famous potato salad. Speaker_2: (Taking a seat) Smells amazing, Bridget! And you remembered my nut allergy with the tart, thank you. Yes, potato salad is here, ready to be devoured. Michael, you’ve massively outdone yourself today. Speaker_3: (Chuckling) Always a pleasure to feed a hungry family. Though, honestly, I think you’re more discerning critics than any restaurant. Bridget, that tart looks fantastic. Speaker_1: Don’t be silly, Michael. It’s a simple recipe, really. I find myself trying out more things now I've retired. Keeps the brain ticking, you know. Though I’m still trying to convince the choir to let me lead a session on mathematical musical ratios. They’re not entirely convinced it’s relevant! Speaker_2: (Laughing) Mathematical musical ratios? That’s brilliant, Aunt Bridget! You’re incorrigible. How’s the choir going otherwise? Are you finally nailing that high note in ‘Amazing Grace’? Speaker_1: Not quite, dear. Still a work in progress! But the director seems pleased overall. It's lovely to be surrounded by music again. And socialising, of course. It's important to stay active and meet people. Though, someone should teach young people the importance of punctuality! That grandson of yours was nearly half an hour late tonight. Speaker_2: (Sighing) Tell me about it! Honestly, he thinks time is some sort of elastic concept. I keep telling him it's important for respect, for everyone's time… It doesn’t sink in. I had to keep chasing his messages. Speaker_3: (Shaking his head) Typical boy. They all think they’re entitled to run on their own clock. When I was a lad, if you were late, you faced the music! Teachers used to be much stricter. Mr. Davies, my maths teacher, would have had you cleaning the blackboard for a week! Speaker_1: (Smiling ruefully) Oh, those days are gone. They’re so focused on sensitivity these days. Though, I did once have a student who’d deliberately arrive late every Tuesday. Drove me mad. Speaker_1: Right, so I was thinking, you’ve got to beat this one, alright? It's brutal. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Alright, alright. Lay it on me. Prepared to be humbled. Speaker_1: Okay. Speaker_1: Right, so let’s run through this planning application one last time. I’m feeling a bit twitchy about it, to be honest. Speaker_2: Twitchy how? It’s a straightforward objection, really. Speaker_1: Excuse me, do you happen to know where the seminar room for the Archaeology panel is? Speaker_2: Oh, definitely! It’s just down this corridor, third door on the left. Professor Alistair Finch, from the History department. I used to lecture here. These hallowed halls have seen a great many changes over the years, you know. Speaker_2: It’s wonderful to meet you, Professor Finch. I think my supervisor occasionally mentions your lectures. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Well, I hope he mentions them positively! I did spend a good few years in the Middle East, excavating a small, lost village near Palmyra. The pottery shards alone told a fascinating story of trade and cultural exchange. I often joked with my team that we were chasing ghosts of conversations. Speaker_2: That sounds incredible! Was it difficult to get funding for projects like that? Speaker_3: Always! Archaeology, particularly in less-visited regions, faces constant funding challenges. But the insights you gain... well, that’s invaluable. I remember once, we unearthed a series of clay tablets with inscriptions in something akin to early Aramaic. It gave us a completely new perspective on the village's trading networks. Speaker_1: Are you familiar with the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis at all, Professor? The idea that the structure of a language influences the way its speakers perceive the world? Speaker_3: Of course! A fascinating, though somewhat contentious, theory. Though I believe the arguments for language's influence on cognition have strengthened over the years. I’m always interested to hear peoples’ perspectives on languages and their connection to ways of thinking. Speaker_2: It's definitely something I grapple with in my work. My current project is focusing on how dialectal variations influence the interpretation of legal documents. It’s complex. Speaker_1: I bet! Speaking of languages, have either of you had a chance to try any Chinese? Mandarin, specifically? Speaker_3: I dipped my toes in, years ago. A most challenging language! The tonal system alone… quite daunting. Far easier to appreciate from a historical perspective, I've found. Speaker_2: I've thought about taking classes, but it feels so far removed from what I do!

Nicely executed. Speaker_1: It just feels like everyone's chasing views these days. My mate Liam is convinced he's going to be famous on TikTok. He's doing these… really obscure historical reenactments. Speaker_2: Like what? Speaker_1: Like, the Battle of Hastings, but he’s wearing a ripped hoodie and using a skateboard as a shield. It’s… something. But I don’t know if it’s going to launch him to stardom. Speaker_3: Bless him. It’s that whole pressure, isn't it? To be constantly creating content, to be noticed. I worry about these young kids, honestly. And the education system just doesn’t seem to cater to it. My cousin's struggling with dyslexia at uni, and the support is just… insufficient. Speaker_4: You're right about that. It's almost as if they expect everyone to learn the same way, at the same pace. Class plays a huge part in that too, doesn't it? Have you looked at our investments lately? I feel like we should be doing something more proactive. Speaker_1: (Frowning) I’ve been meaning to. Things felt a bit shaky last time I checked. Speaking of switching off, I was thinking we could have that weekend away we talked about. Just you and me. Somewhere quiet. No lectures, no physios, no government pronouncements. Speaker_1: This lentil soup is absolutely divine, isn’t it? Honestly, I think it's the best I’ve ever made. Speaker_2: It is lovely, Mum. Really warming. Perfect for a chilly day like this. Speaker_1: So, how was the Lego today, Finn? Did you finish building that spaceship? Speaker_2: Nearly, Dad. I’m just adding the wings now. It’s really complicated, you know. Speaker_1: Right then, who’s bringing the sprouts this year? Don’t want a repeat of last year's sprout catastrophe. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, Arthur! You and your sprouts. I’ll do them, dear. Speaker_1: Right, so I’ve got the lasagne bubbling away nicely. Anyone want a glass of wine while we chat? Speaker_3: Yes please! White, if you’ve got it. Feeling a bit… celebratory. That would mean new borders basically, although they've said they'd want to maintain close ties with the rest of the UK. Travel would likely change, require passports possibly, at least initially. Speaker_1: That’s one of the really complicated bits. They'd have to decide that. Speaker_1: Aye, they’d need to build up their own defence forces, or enter into some sort of agreement with other countries. It’s a massive undertaking. And what about things like healthcare and education - how would those be funded and run differently? Speaker_2: It sounds like a lot of hassle. Don’t they share resources now? Like, does England benefit from Scotland, or vice versa? Speaker_1: Well, that's another key debate, isn’t it? There's arguments both ways. Speaker_1: Your welcome, love. You are a proper star. Eating up all that Yorkshire Pudding! Speaker_2: Haha. Speaker_1: Good eating is good, isn't it? Speaker_2: Yeah! Very good! Speaker_1: (Entering the kitchen, dropping a bag of pastries onto the counter with a sigh) Oh my god, I need a cup of tea. Paris was… a lot. Speaker_2: (Standing at the stove, stirring something in a pan) Welcome back, darling! You look exhausted. Everything alright? And what are those, they smell divine. Thought you’d be hungry after all that walking, even if it was slightly painful walking! How was the hotel? Fancy? Speaker_1: Pretty swanky, actually. Right near the Louvre. But the shower was the size of a shoebox. Seriously. You could barely turn around. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Classic Paris! Tiny showers, huge pastries. It's the law. Speaker_1: Exactly! And also, Sarah bailed on us last minute. Speaker_2: What? Sarah? Why? Speaker_1: She said her cat went into labour. Apparently, it's a very dramatic feline. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) Oh, Sarah. Always an excuse. Speaker_1: I know! Left us hanging! We ended up having to navigate the metro with a dodgy map and my dodgy ankle. It was chaotic. I nearly missed my flight. Speaker_2: Oh, darling, that sounds dreadful. I’m glad you’re back safe and sound. Though I do feel bad about Sarah. Cats are family, you know. Speaker_1: I get it! But seriously, I was so stressed. And the French waiters, they're just… something else. Eye rolls and sighs everywhere. Speaker_3: You’re exaggerating! I went to Paris last year, the waiters were perfectly charming. Speaker_1: You always say that! You're a natural diplomat, Chloe. I don’t have your patience. One guy practically threw my croissant at me. Speaker_2: (Smiling) You’re just being dramatic. Now, sit down, have some soup, and tell me everything. Did you get any good pictures? And did you buy any perfume? Speaker_1: (Sinking into a chair) Okay, okay. Soup sounds amazing right now. The pictures are… a work in progress. And yes, I got some perfume. A ridiculously expensive, tiny bottle of something that smells like lilies and regret. But it was a souvenir! And I'll show you tomorrow. First, more pastries and that soup please! Mum, you are a saviour! Speaker_3: So when are you going to get a shoe that doesn't rub you ankle raw. Speaker_1: I’ll look. Right now I need to rest and forget I was ever in Paris.H.H..

Speaker_1: Hey Chloe! Fancy seeing you here before the linguistics seminar. Didn’t realize you were heading this way. Speaker_2: Hey Ben! We haven't been seeing each other, not really. He proposed a while back, but… (trails off). It just wasn't right. How's your own relationship shaping up? Speaker_2: It's good. Really good. We're thinking of getting a flat together, actually. Big step. My brother's just gone through a divorce though. It's a right mess, to be honest. Loads of lawyers and fireworks flying around. Speaker_1: Oh wow, that sounds awful. Sorry to hear that. Well, I best get going. Need to try and decipher the mysteries of the passive voice before Professor Davies decides I haven’t a clue what I’m talking about. Good luck with your seminar! Speaker_2: You too! And seriously, consider *Hamilton*. You won't regret it. See you around! Maybe we can grab coffee sometime next week – de-stress after the seminar, you know? Speaker_1: Sounds good! Definitely. Later! Speaker_2: Bye Ben!H.H..

Speaker_2: Right, so first things first, you’ve got to rinse the rice. Really well. Like, until the water runs clear almost. See? Like that. Speaker_1: Why? Speaker_2: Because otherwise it’ll be all starchy and gluggy, right? No one wants gluggy rice. It needs to be fluffy. Like…like clouds, almost. Speaker_1: Clouds aren’t exactly fluffy, are they? They're just…big. Speaker_2: (chuckles) Okay, fair point. Like…puffy pillows, then. Puffy pillows of rice. There you go. Now, into the pan. Speaker_1: How much water do I need? Speaker_2: Right, now this is important. For a cup of rice… twice the amount of water. So two cups. Roughly. Watch me. See? You don’t need to be exact, honestly. Speaker_1: Two cups. Right. Speaker_2: Okay, pop it on a medium heat. Don’t crank it up high, or it’ll just boil over and make a mess. And then… don't touch it. Leave it. Speaker_1: Leave it? For how long? Speaker_2: About 18-20 minutes. Keep an eye on it though. You’ll see little bubbles starting, and then it’ll quieten down. When it’s quiet, it's probably done. But, you can lift the lid and poke it with a fork just to be sure. Speaker_1: And then what? Speaker_2: Then, turn the heat off. And crucially… don’t stir it! Just leave it covered for another five minutes. It needs to steam. That's what makes it fluffy. Speaker_1: So, just rinsing, water, heat, wait, don’t stir. Got it. Speaker_2: Exactly! Now, while that’s doing its thing, let's get the curry going. We can use those vouchers we got, right? Speaker_1: Yeah, for that Indian place. But I don’t really like anything too spicy. Speaker_2: Okay, okay. We’ll get something mild, then. I'm thinking…butter chicken? It’s always a winner. And loads of naan bread to soak up the sauce. Speaker_1: Sounds good! Speaker_2: Now look, remember what happened last week with the meat? Don’t leave it out on the counter for ages, okay? It’s best to cook it straight away or put it in the fridge. Honestly, you can smell when it’s going off. Speaker_1: Yeah, it smelled a bit funny. Speaker_2: Exactly! And remember when we were talking about those documentaries about food? All that salt and fat… It’s scary, isn’t it? Speaker_1: Are jalapenos bad for you? Speaker_2: Well, they’re spicy, right? So, they're good for giving you a bit of a kick. But, too many and you might get...well, you know. A dodgy tummy. Speaker_1: My friend’s little brother had a really weird birthmark on his face. It didn’t look right, did it? Speaker_2: Oh, bless him. Some people are just born with things, aren't they? Like jellyfish. You know, some jellyfish sting, some don’t. You can’t always tell. Speaker_1: That's weird. Speaker_2: Life’s weird. Now, focus! Rice is bubbling! Have a look.H...

Speaker_1: (Pushing peas around his plate) This’ll be another week of beans on toast, then. Speaker_2: Don’t be like that, Liam. Mum’s put in a right effort. And it's better than nothing. Speaker_1: Aye, I know, I know. Just... feeling a bit down, that's all. Another rejection letter today. "Highly competitive field…" blaa blaa blaa. Speaker_4: Don't let it get to you, Liam. You’ve got a degree, you’re smart. Something’ll turn up. Did you apply for that assistant role down at the library again? Speaker_1: Aye, did. Didn't even get an interview. They said they've gone with someone who has "relevant experience." What relevant experience does a philosophy degree give you, eh? Thinking about stuff? Speaker_3: (Laughing) Proper deep thoughts, Liam. Speaker_1: Exactly! Deep, useless thoughts, that's what. Speaker_2: It's just, you’re so focused on work. What about that coding course you were looking at? Speaker_1: Nah, can't afford it. Not even with Mum's help. Every penny's going on bills, isn't it? Speaker_4: True. Mum’s struggling too, isn’t she? I'm worried about her, actually. The care home bills... Speaker_2: Don’t go there, Sarah. Let’s just enjoy dinner. Speaker_3: Speaking of which, it's actually really good, Mum! Thanks. Even the peas. Speaker_1: See? Someone appreciates it. Speaker_2: What did you get up to at college today, Elodie? Anything interesting? Speaker_3: Miss Thompson grilled us on Romantic poetry again. Honestly, I'm half convinced she just likes hearing herself talk. Speaker_4: You should’ve told her! Speaker_3: I wanted to, but… you know. Teachers. Speaker_1: Remember Mrs. Grimshaw back in school? The geography one? She used to fall asleep during her own lessons. Speaker_2: (Chuckling) Oh my god, yes! I totally forgot about that. She'd be snoring away, and we’d be passing notes. Speaker_4: Bless her. It was a tough time for her, wasn't it? She lost her husband around then. Speaker_1: Aye, poor woman. School was never the same. Did you see that new series on Netflix, “The Ridge?” Speaker_2: Oh, yeah! I'm hooked! The acting’s brilliant, and the scenery is gorgeous. Speaker_4: I started it, but it's a bit intense for me, to be honest. Too many dodgy characters. Speaker_3: My friend, Chloe, said it's the new "Line of Duty!" Speaker_1: "Line of Duty" was brilliant though. Proper gripping. Makes you think, doesn’t it? Just like my philosophy degree… (He says it sarcastically). Speaker_2: Don't start again, Liam! How’s Carl doing? Did you hear back from him about that gig? Speaker_1: No, nothing. He's been quiet as a mouse. Probably forgotten all about me helping him move that piano last month. Speaker_4: He’s probably just busy. Don't worry about it. There'll be other chances. And speaking of chances, I've got a job interview next week! Speaker_2: No way! That’s brilliant, Sarah! Where is it? Speaker_4: The community centre, for an outreach support worker role. Helping vulnerable adults. Speaker_3: That’s amazing, Sarah. You’ll be brilliant at it. Speaker_1: Proper good for you, lass. Should be getting a decent wage, too. Be able to help out a bit then. Speaker_4: Don't get ahead of yourself! I haven't even got the job yet. But

Speaker_2: This shepherd's pie is really good, by the way. Proper comfort food. Speaker_1: Aye, it is reet good, isn't it? Glad you like it. Mum always made the best. Could eat this every night, honestly. Speaker_2: Proper hearty. So, you said you were dealing with a bit of a nightmare at work? With the conference? Speaker_1: Oh, you have no idea. It's the caterers. Absolutely useless. They promised me Yorkshire puddings for the Yorkshire-themed evening and they’ve sent over… mini quiches. Mini quiches! Speaker_2: (Laughs) Yorkshire puddings and mini quiches are not a match made in heaven, are they? Speaker_1: Exactly! It’s supposed to be a celebration of Yorkshire. It’s like serving Haggis at a Burns Night supper! You know? Speaker_2: Absolutely. That’s a massive faux pas. What are you going to do now? Speaker_1: I’m trying to sort it. I’ve called them, had a right barney with them. They’re trying to say it’s “supply chain issues.” Supply chain issues for Yorkshire puddings? Seriously? Speaker_2: They’re having a laugh, aren’t they? Do you have any other caterers you could quickly get in? Speaker_1: That’s what I’m looking at. Problem is, the conference is tomorrow. Everything’s booked, everyone’s arriving. Changing things last minute is a nightmare. Speaker_2: Business life. Never dull, eh? Speaker_1: No, it's definitely not. Although sometimes I wish it was. I’m thinking of having a real proper proper go at that yoga studio. The one down the road. Speaker_2: Oh, really? The one you mentioned a few weeks ago? You should! Get some of that stress out. Speaker_1: I know, I know. I’ve been putting it off. Just feel like I don't have the time, but then I realise I do. I just make excuses. Speaker_2: We all do. I spent most of my time last week trying to teach myself to juggle. Speaker_1: (Laughs) You? Juggling? Speaker_2: Yeah! I thought it’d be a good way to pass the time. Let's just say I'm sticking to watching telly for now. Dropped one on my foot. Speaker_1: Oh, you poor thing! See, that is a good reason to avoid juggling though. Maybe yoga's less likely to cause injury. Speaker_2: Definitely less likely. You need to move your body a bit though, don't you? Sitting at a desk all day… Speaker_1: I know, I know. It's just been the last few weeks have been manic. The conference prep, the flat hunting... Speaker_2: Oh, the flat! How's that going? Did you find anything decent? Speaker_1: Not really. Everything’s either tiny or extortionate. I saw one the other day that was the size of a cupboard, and the landlord wanted a year’s rent upfront. Speaker_2: Bonkers! Seems like Cambridge is getting even more ridiculous. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. I might have to reconsider moving further out, but then the commute’s a nightmare. It's a constant compromise isn’t it? Speaker_2: All the time. At least you're having a laugh with it, eh? Look, you’re doing alright. Just keep chipping away. And book that yoga class! Promise me. Speaker_1: Alright, alright. I'll book it. You're right. A bit of stretching probably wouldn't go amiss. I've got that, like, posture of someone who spends their life hunched over a laptop.

Speaker_1: Right, so, dishes. Who’s on it? Speaker_2: I'll do it. Speaker_3: No, let me do it, mate. You two clear the table, yeah? Speaker_4: Fine. Speaker_1: Thanks, love. Speaker_3: He’s got a good serve, haven't you? Speaker_2: Yeah, but he’s got no control. Flapping all over the place. Speaker_4: Not as good as me, though. Speaker_2: Oh, shut up. Speaker_2: It looks daft. Speaker_4: My mate Ben’s grown a beard. He looks like a Viking. Speaker_3: Does he now? Instagram’s full of beards these days, isn't it? Speaker_1: It is. Though I don’t understand why anyone would want to look like a lumberjack. Speaker_2: Liam’s posting loads of pictures of his girlfriend. Speaker_3: Is he? Good for him. About time, I thought. Speaker_1: She seems lovely. Does she like tennis as well? Speaker_2: Nah, she’s into… dance or something. TikTok stuff. Speaker_4: Don’t be mean. Speaker_2: I’m not being mean! It’s just… different. Speaker_3: Well, everyone’s different. As long as he’s happy. Speaking of TikTok, are you two still glued to your phones? Speaker_4: It’s not glued! Speaker_2: We only look at it for like, five minutes. Speaker_1: Five minutes turns into an hour, you know. You need to do other things. Read a book, play tennis… Speaker_3: (Laughing) Or clear the dishes! Speaker_2: Honestly, Dad, you’re such a nag. Speaker_3: Someone's got to be. Just remember, the real world isn't on Instagram. Speaker_1: Right, so we need to sort out the sofa before Christmas definitely. I’m thinking maybe DFS? They’ve got those two-for-one deals on again. Speaker_2: Yeah, that's probably the best bet. I thought they charged for big stuff now. Speaker_1: They do, but it’s cheaper than renting a skip. And we should probably clear out some of those unwanted presents while we're at it, don't you think? All that Christmas tat. Speaker_3: Don't you dare throw away that ceramic robin! Your Grandad bought that for me! Speaker_1: (Laughing) Mum, you haven’t looked at that robin in fifteen years! It’s been gathering dust in the attic. Speaker_2: Speaking of family, what’s happening with Emily? Has she found a place yet? Speaker_1: Not really. She’s still looking. It's so difficult to find anything decent at a reasonable price. Especially with all that new building going on. Speaker_3: All these new houses... They could do with some green spaces. It’s just concrete everywhere. Speaker_2: Honestly, I hate when people wash your clothes. Like, who does that?! Speaker_1: Tell me about it! It’s just… weird. Why would you need to clean someone else's socks? Speaker_3: Your great-aunt Mabel used to do that. She had a swear box, though. If you said a bad word, she'd make you put a penny in it. Speaker_1: Wow! It’s just… what did she do with all the money? Speaker_3: Bought more ceramic robins, probably! Speaker_2: (Laughs) What about the beaver scouts Christmas party? Are you going to volunteer? Speaker_1: I’m thinking about it. It’ll be manic, though. Lots of sticky fingers and excited shouting. Speaker_3: Your cousin, David, he used to be a Beaver Scout. Remember? The little rascal used to get into all sorts of mischief. Speaker_2: Oh, good point. You've been neglecting it. We could do that in the afternoon, if the den-building doesn't take all day. Speaker_1: (Eyes glued to the screen, pausing the film briefly) Right, this scene’s mental, isn't it? Proper Tarantino. Speaker_2: (Leaning back on the sofa, a mug of tea in hand) Yeah, it's good. Speaker_1: So, tell me everything! How’s the new job going, love? Really going? Speaker_2: It’s… a lot, Mum. Honestly. But good! The kids are lovely, really lovely. I've already started thinking about decorations and food. Should we do a buffet or a sit-down meal? Speaker_1: Buffet's always easier, isn’t it? Less stress. We can get some of those little sausage rolls that everyone loves, and a big bowl of salad. Speaker_2: Sounds good. And definitely need those mini quiches. Grandma loves them. Speaker_1: Absolutely. Right, let's look at dates then, shall we? What about the 16th? That’s a Saturday, everyone should be free. Speaker_2: The 16th is perfect. I’ll book the photographer then. He'll be running around with his shoes off, of course, but still. It’s going to be lovely. I'm glad I came to see you today, Mum. I needed a chat. Speaker_1: Always here for you, love. Always.

Speaker_1: It’s so lovely to finally see you, Sarah! It feels like ages. This house is gorgeous by the way, really cosy. Speaker_2: Oh, darling, it's wonderful to see you too, Chloe! Brings a whole new meaning to Christmas dinner, doesn't it? Explaining all the molecular structures! Speaker_1: (Laughs) I can imagine! Though, honestly, my family’s Christmas dinner conversations usually revolve around whether Auntie Brenda remembered to buy the cranberry sauce *again*. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, Brenda! Some things never change. Speaking of families, how are your parents? Still battling the garden? Speaker_1: They are! Mum’s convinced she’s going to win the Village Flower Competition this year. Speaker_2: Just natural stuff, you know, lotions and creams. I've been experimenting for ages, using essential oils and things. Restorative stuff for mature skin, you know. I even got a little certificate in formulating! I've been thinking of selling them at the local markets. Speaker_1: That’s amazing! You're so clever. You should definitely do it. There’s a huge market for that kind of thing. Natural, handmade… people love it. You could even sell them online! Speaker_2: I’ve been thinking about Etsy. It's a bit daunting though, isn't it? All the marketing, the shipping... Speaker_1: It can be, but it’s doable. I know a couple of people who do really well with it. It's important to present it nicely, good photos, clear descriptions… Speaker_2: Exactly! I just need to take the plunge. Oh, and Rusty’s been getting a bit grey around the muzzle. I'm really worried about him, you know. He is my best mate. Speaker_1: Aw, poor Rusty! Dogs are family, aren’t they? I hope

Speaker_1: (Reaching for a piece of charoset) This is incredible, honestly. Yours is always the best. Seriously, your great-grandmother's recipe? Speaker_2: (Smiling proudly) Yeah, it is. Though I've tweaked it a bit over the years, obviously. More walnuts this year, I think. More cinnamon. You need that warmth, you know, for Passover. Speaker_3: (Adjusting her glasses) It *is* exceptional, darling. The consistency is perfect. Not too gluey, not too crumbly. It’s got that… je ne sais quoi. Speaker_4: (Chuckling) "Je ne sais quoi" at a Passover Seder. Classic Mum. Speaker_3: Well, it has! It's the balance. And the apples… Granny Smiths, naturally. Speaker_1: Granny Smiths are key. You know, Liam was asking me the other day about the whole Seder plate thing. All the symbolic food. Speaker_2: Oh really? What did you tell him? Speaker_1: Well, I tried to explain the matzah, you know, the unleavened bread, representing the haste of the Exodus… Speaker_4: (Interrupting with a grin) …and the burning desire to get away from Pharaoh’s awful bread! Speaker_3: (Laughing) Oh, Adam, you and your jokes. But it’s true, the matzah does symbolize the lack of time. And the maror – the horseradish – represents the bitterness of slavery. Speaker_2: It *is* quite bitter, isn’t it? I always think someone should invent a slightly less intense version. It's a bit much for some people. Speaker_1: Maybe a balsamic reduction? Sweeten it a bit? Speaker_3: (Making a face) Absolutely not! That would be sacrilege! It has to be properly bitter. It’s part of the experience. Speaking of experiences, I’m thinking of finally doing that Jewish food tour of Italy next year. Speaker_4: Italy? Seriously? Which part? Speaker_3: Rome, mainly. There’s a surprisingly rich Jewish history there. And of course, the food! I’ve heard the fried artichokes are divine. Speaker_2: Oh my gosh, yes! And the carciofi alla giudia… you have to try them. We talked about going with you! Speaker_1: I'm definitely in for that! We need to start planning. Maybe spring of '25? Before everyone's dates get too crazy. Speaker_4: Sounds amazing. Actually, I was looking at flights to New York the other day… thinking about finally visiting that Katz's Delicatessen. Speaker_3: Katz's! Of course! You must go. Do you know the story of how they came up with the name? Speaker_4: No, tell me! Speaker_3: It’s quite a tale... involved a particularly grumpy customer and a very unfortunate incident with a potato… (starts to launch into a story) Speaker_2: (Cutting in gently) Mum, maybe later? We're getting to the Afikoman hunt, and Liam’s already eyeing up the chocolates. Speaker_1: Yeah, we don’t want to keep him waiting! By the way, did you ever finish reading that essay about Ortolan? It was brilliant… though a little grim. Speaker_3: Oh yes, the Ortolan. A truly stomach-churning tradition. The last bird – eating it, feathers and all, under a napkin... Speaker_4: (Slightly queasy) Right, well, let’s focus on the charoset. And the lovely, perfectly bitter horseradish. Speaker_2: (Laughing) You’ll be alright, Adam! Pass the matzah ball soup then. And everyone, remember to sing “Echad Mi Yodea”? Speaker_1: (Grinning) Of course! Who knows one?

Speaker_1: Right, so, who's ready to absolutely demolish "The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo"? I'm still reeling from it. Speaker_2: Oh, honestly, Sarah, I’m still having trouble processing. It was just…a lot, wasn't it? Proper page-turner though, couldn’t put it down, even when I should have been prepping for tomorrow's budget meeting. Speaker_3: Totally agree! I was up way too late last night. I think I finished it around 2 am. I kept thinking, "Just one more chapter…" and then bam, Evelyn’s whole life unfolded. Did anyone else find the ending completely devastating? Speaker_1: Devastating is putting it mildly! And the whole unreliable narrator thing! Clever, clever writing. I’m gutted it's finished, though. What shall we read next? Speaker_2: Ooh, I was thinking something lighter after that emotional rollercoaster. Something cosy. Perhaps a Dorothy Sayers? Speaker_3: Dorothy Sayers? Bit heavy for me after that, I think. Maybe something by Kate Morton? I loved "The Forgotten Garden." Atmospheric and a bit spooky. Speaker_1: Kate Morton is always a good shout. Though, I'm feeling a bit…knitting-inspired this month. Has anyone read any books *about* knitting? Seems silly, I know. I’ve just finished a giant chunky cardigan - pure catharsis after that book! Speaker_2: Knitting, eh? You know, my grandmother used to knit these incredible Argyle jumpers. She even had patterns for little matching ones for us grandkids. Such a shame those skills are disappearing. I tried to learn once, but I'm absolutely hopeless. I ended up with a tangled mess and a very frustrated cat. Speaker_3: My mum's a crochet whiz. She makes the most amazing blankets and throws. I’m trying to pick it up but I'm hopeless at keeping the tension right. Always ending up with wonky edges. Speaker_1: Wonky edges have character! Honestly, embrace the imperfections. It’s part of the charm. Speaking of charm, have you all seen "Succession"? Speaker_2: Oh, "Succession"! Absolutely brilliant. The writing, the acting... It's just so deliciously cynical. Although, I do occasionally shout at the telly. It's terribly stressful watching them all be awful to each other! Speaker_3: I'm hooked! I love how they manage to make morally questionable people so compelling. Plus, that soundtrack is incredible. I’ve been listening to it on Spotify non-stop. Actually, talking of listening, does anyone actually *read* books anymore, or are you all e-readers now? Speaker_1: Oh, I'm staunchly old-school. I love the feel of a book, the smell of the paper… It's a sensory experience. My Kindle gathers dust. Although, I did get a fantastic deal on a box set of Agatha Christie eBooks. Couldn’t resist! Speaker_2: I used to be all about physical books, but I caved a few years ago. Easier for travel, definitely. Plus, you can adjust the font size, which is a godsend for these aging eyes. Speaker_3: I’m mostly eBooks these days. It's just so convenient. I’m always on the go, and I can carry a whole library on my phone. Do you think it impacts how we read though? Are we less focused, constantly checking emails and notifications? Speaker_1: That’s a very good point. I do find myself distracted sometimes. Maybe that’s why I’ve been knitting so much - it forces me to focus on one thing. Speaker_2: Speaking of distractions, anyone seen that new film adaptation of "Little Women"? Apparently, it’s stunning. Speaker_3: I've heard great things! Definitely on my list. Need to check showtimes though – the cinema down the road is showing things later and later now. Speaker_1: Oh, I saw it last week. Absolutely gorgeous. Saoirse Ronan is brilliant, as is Florence Pugh. Proper

Speaker_2: Right, so, the big question – how do I even *turn this thing on?* It’s just… black. Speaker_1: (Chuckles, fiddling with his own phone) Ah, yes. A common predicament with new technology. See that tiny button on the right side? Press and hold it for a few seconds. Should vibrate and the Nokia logo should pop up. Speaker_2: (Presses the button) Yep, vibrate! Logo! Okay, progress. Who knew something so simple could be so daunting? Speaker_1: It’s the Finnish minimalism, love. Nokia prides itself on it. Less is more, you know? Though I do miss the days of a satisfyingly chunky charger port. These USB-C things are a pain. Speaker_2: Tell me about it. I’m already dreading accidentally leaving it somewhere. Right, now it's asking for a language… obviously English, yeah? Speaker_1: Absolutely. And then you'll be prompted to set up your Google account. Or a Nokia account, if you’re feeling particularly adventurous. Speaker_2: Google, definitely. Is it easy to transfer all my stuff from my old phone? I’ve got loads of photos and… well, everything, really. Speaker_1: It should be. They have a handy little Google Drive backup system. Just make sure your old phone is connected to Wi-Fi and you follow the prompts. They’ll walk you through it. Honestly, it's much easier than it used to be. Remember when you had to root around with cables and computer software? Speaker_2: Oh god, don't remind me! My dad used to think he was a computer genius trying to do that. A lot of frustration and very little success. Speaker_1: (Laughs) Sounds about right. Now, let’s see, do you want me to help you with the Wi-Fi connection? This pub's Wi-Fi is… questionable, to say the least. Speaker_2: Please! I’m utterly clueless. I’ve got the password, but it’s not connecting. Speaker_1: Right. Let me just… (Taps away on his phone) Okay, it’s being a bit temperamental, but I think I’ve got it. Try it now? Speaker_2: (Tries) Yes! It’s working! Thank you. You’re a lifesaver. I feel like I've conquered a small mountain. Speaker_1: Don’t mention it. This is what older brothers are for, isn't it? Though, I’m still baffled as to why you chose a Nokia after being so loyal to Apple for so long. Speaker_2: I know, right? It was a bit impulsive, I confess. But I just… liked the design, I guess. And the slightly ridiculous idea of having a super-robust, practically indestructible phone while travelling around Finland. Plus, I got it at a bargain price. Speaker_1: A sensible decision, then. Although, be warned, the camera isn’t quite as spectacular as the iPhone. Still, you’ll take some stunning photos of the Northern Lights, I hope! Speaker_2: Fingers crossed! Okay, next hurdle – setting up the apps. Do you think I should just download everything from the Play Store? Speaker_1: Exactly. And be selective! Don't feel compelled to download every single app just because it's available. You'll just clutter up the phone and drain the battery. Speaker_2: Good point. I get sucked in, don't I? Okay, messaging apps first, definitely. And Google Maps, obviously. I don't want to get wildly lost in the Finnish wilderness.H.,..

Speaker_2: So, what’s your favourite animal then, love? Apart from Finn, of course. Speaker_1: Hmm, that’s a tough one. Probably a Red Panda. They’re so fluffy. Did you know they're actually more closely related to raccoons than pandas? Speaker_2: No! Really? You're full of knowledge. Finn, do you know what a Red Panda is? (Finn gurgles and points vaguely towards a picture book.) Speaker_1: He likes the dogs better, I think. You know, like Malamooches. Speaker_2: Oh, those big fluffy dogs! Those are proper characters, aren't they? Remember when we saw that one in Bristol, pulling a little kid on a scooter? Speaker_1: Yeah! It was massive. Bigger than me, almost. My cat, Jasper, would be terrified. Speaker_2: Jasper's a brave little thing, really. He’d probably hiss at a Malamooche. Speaker_1: Probably. Anyway, about Liam’s birthday… what are we doing? His party’s this weekend, remember? Speaker_2: Yes, already! It’s flying by. I was thinking maybe board games, and we could set up a little gymnastics area in the garden, if the weather’s good. Speaker_1: Yeah, good idea! He loves gymnastics. Maybe we can get him that new balancing beam he wanted? Speaker_2: We can look. It's a bit pricey, though. We’ll have to pop into the shops later. Speaking of shops, we need to think about holidays. Are we thinking of going back to England this year? Speaker_1: I really want to see Grandma again and Granpa. And maybe go to that Japanese film festival in Bristol. They’re showing all my favourites. Speaker_2: I’d love that. We just need to figure out the timings and who can look after Finn. He’s getting so big and independent! Speaker_1: He is! He can almost say ‘Red Panda’ now. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Honestly, he's a little genius. He’s become obsessed with my iPad recently. Keeps trying to swipe it. Speaker_1: He’ll be using a laptop before you know it! We have to get him some kind of educational apps. Speaker_2: Absolutely. We want to keep him entertained, but not just stuck on screens all the time. How about we try and find him some of those big, chunky children’s books? You know, the ones with the really nice illustrations? Speaker_1: Yeah! And maybe that poem we read last week? About the little bear? Speaker_2: That was lovely. We should definitely get him that one. Okay, so to recap: board games, gymnastics, puzzle for Emily, Japanese film festival in Bristol... and lots of Red Pandas! Speaker_1: Sounds perfect! Now, can we play Scrabble?
